articles.title: Abu Dhabi launches a wildlife rescue network
articles.body: A sea turtle in shallow water; a photograph accompanying the announcement of the Abu Dhabi Wildlife Response Network. The release of 76 turtles at Saadiyat Beach accompanies the network’s launch. The Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi (EAD) has launched the Abu Dhabi Wildlife Response Network to coordinate reports, interventions and animal care with partners and the community. Its announcement was published on 17 October 2026. The launch was accompanied by the release of 76 hawksbill and green sea turtles at Saadiyat Beach following treatment and rehabilitation, according to EAD. The agency said its joint efforts with partners had returned more than 1,500 turtles to Abu Dhabi’s waters over several years. From reporting to rehabilitation Cases are recorded and assessed before a specialist team intervenes, stabilising the animal if necessary and transferring it for veterinary care. Release follows recovery, while animals needing further attention remain in care. Experience predating the network Field work has an earlier history: the joint rescue programme with The National Aquarium began in August 2020. In 2023, EAD explained that some released turtles carried tracking devices, while a rehabilitation area in the waters around Louvre Abu Dhabi provided care before release. Protecting animals and their habitat EAD lists abandoned fishing nets, marine debris, pollution and coastal development among the threats to green turtles, alongside the importance of avoiding boat strikes. Protecting waters and beaches therefore remains complementary to animal rescue. At Saadiyat, the Emirates Nature-WWF guide asks visitors to keep a safe distance from marine wildlife and avoid feeding it. It lists 800-555 for reporting sightings, strandings and pollution, and response@ead.gov.ae as the rescue network’s email address. articles.title: Alpine Accentor
articles.body: Alpine Accentor Prunella collaris Identity, life and distribution Alpine Accentor Prunella collaris inhabits rocky uplands and mountain grassland. The scientific name helps avoid confusion with Dunnock and other small birds that may look superficially similar. It searches the ground among rocks and grass. Invertebrates are part of its diet, with seeds becoming more important as seasons change. Winter movements may involve descending to lower elevations rather than a regular long-distance migration. The nest is concealed in a rock fissure. Females may associate with more than one male in mating and chick care, so a small group cannot automatically be interpreted as a single pair and its young. Its range includes mountains of the Maghreb, as described by the Cévennes National Park account. This does not imply occurrence in every Arab mountain range. Record place, elevation and date without disturbing birds or searching for nests. A 2023 study in Evolution supports breeding populations in Morocco through comparison of Moroccan and Spanish samples. www.bto.org — Alpine Accentor · www.oiseaux.net — Alpine Accentor · biodiversite.cevennes-parcnational.fr — Alpine Accentor · academic.oup.com — Alpine Accentor Photo: Paulo Caseirito

articles.title: Arabian Green Bee-eater
articles.body: Arabian Green Bee-eater Merops cyanophrys Identity and identification Arabian Green Bee-eater Merops cyanophrys belongs to Meropidae. Green plumage, a black eye stripe, conspicuous blue face and throat and elongated adult central tail feathers characterise it. It was split from the former green bee-eater complex; old Merops orientalis photographs require geographic and diagnostic checks. It is placed in the order Coraciiformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Wadis, farmland, gardens and dry country with exposed perches provide habitat. It sallies for flying insects and often returns to a perch. Bees, wasps and other flying insects are eaten; the name does not imply exclusive dependence on managed honeybees. Breeding and parental care It excavates a nesting tunnel in suitable soil, ending in an internal chamber. Adults bring insects to the young. A stable bank or small earth face is important for nesting success. Never expose a chamber or insert an object into the tunnel to check occupancy. Range and Arab occurrence Associated with Arabia and the southern Levant, it occurs in Saudi Arabia, Oman, Yemen and adjoining areas. The Birds of AlUla guide documents Saudi occurrence, supported by Omani and Jordanian observations. Its range differs from African and Asian green bee-eaters formerly combined with it. Seasonality and observation It is resident across suitable parts of its Arab range, with local movements following food. November observations need not imply long-distance migration. Dated, accurately located photographs help distinguish resident groups from movements beyond usual sites. Ecological role and conservation It consumes flying insects and requires perches and safe earthen nesting sites. Pesticides, bank levelling and nest disturbance degrade habitat. Near apiaries, site management and documented feeding behaviour are preferable to assuming damage or killing birds. References Royal Commission for AlUla — Birds of AlUla, Arabian Green Bee-eater. articles.title: Asian Houbara — Chlamydotis macqueenii
articles.body: Asian houbaraPhoto: Kudaibergen Amirekul — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. Asian houbara (MacQueen’s bustard) — Chlamydotis macqueenii Range: A sleek desert bird of the bustard family. Its range runs from east of Sinai across Iran and Central Asia to the Gobi Desert in Mongolia; northern populations are partial migrants wintering south toward Pakistan, western India, and parts of the Arabian Peninsula. In the Levant it was historically wider in dry steppe; today it is rare or only a vagrant in the Lebanese context compared with soaring migrants. This entry locks Chlamydotis macqueenii only. The African houbara Chlamydotis undulata—North Africa and the Canary Islands—is a separate species elevated in 2003, paler, with different crest feathers in display and a Maghrebi range, not Asian–Levantine; it must not be mixed with the species treated here. Life cycle and habitat: The male performs a striking visual display: inflating neck feathers and folding the head into a “ruff,” then running in lines or circles around shrubs. Mating is polygynous on the male’s side; the female alone tends the nest. She usually lays 2–4 eggs in an open scrape; incubation lasts about 23 days. Precocial chicks follow the mother. It prefers arid desert and steppe with sparse shrub cover; the diet mixes seeds, berries, and insects, and it can forgo free water when food moisture suffices. Lifestyle: Wary, relying on camouflage and crouching low when approached. When pursued it rises and spirals upward. Sensitive to nesting disturbance by people and livestock. Migration routes avoid the highest mountain chains, as satellite tracking has shown; breeding timing links to local temperatures that trigger spring departure. Asian houbaraPhoto: Harsha Jayaramaiah — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. Hunting status: Across Arab countries, Asian houbara is generally protected and hunting is tightly restricted; the species is globally threatened. In Lebanon, Wild Hunting Law No. 580/2004 limits hunting to quarry species set by the minister; everything else is protected year-round; houbara is not among the permitted quarry in the absence of a current open-season decision. Documented exceptions only within licensed falconry frameworks: in Qatar, Ministerial Decision No. 7 of 2026 lists houbara among species that may be taken with falcons only during a set period (1 September 2026 – 15 February 2027), and bans call-playback devices (Ministry of Environment and Climate Change via Qatar News Agency). In Abu Dhabi, within licensed traditional falconry under Executive Council Decision 5/2021 and Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi notices, houbara may be taken by licensed falconers in defined seasons—without implying that all hunting pathways in the emirate are limited to houbara alone. Conservation status: Globally Vulnerable (VU) with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (BirdLife assessment 2021), owing to declines tied to hunting and habitat degradation. Listed on CITES Appendix I and CMS Appendix II. Captive-breeding and release programs form part of the conservation response across parts of the range. Traits: The male’s display is documented courtship, not invented folklore: neck plumes folded over the head, measured pacing, and a soft breathing sound audible only at close range. Doing without free water is a true desert adaptation. An icon of falconry heritage and of conservation duty alike.

articles.title: With Autumn Migration… How Does the World Protect Birds and Regulate Hunting?
articles.body: Prepared by Sayd | 8 September 2026 Birds that cross the sky carry a story longer than the distance we see. Behind every journey are breeding areas, rest and feeding stops, and places where they spend the winter. What happens at one of those stops can affect an entire journey spanning countries and continents. With the autumn migration season, recent international news and reports offer a picture of the challenges these journeys face, and of the tools used to protect them: scientific research, habitat conservation, hunting regulation, and people’s participation in monitoring. More than half of migratory species are declining On 28 July, the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO) presented results of a global review published in the journal Nature Reviews Biodiversity, with researchers from international institutions including Georgetown University and the Smithsonian Institution. The review finds that 51% of migratory bird species worldwide are declining in numbers. That percentage concerns species that are declining; it does not mean half of all bird numbers have disappeared. Pressures include habitat loss, climate change and extreme weather, pesticides, disease, and collisions with buildings and structures. Researchers therefore call for protection that takes account of the bird’s full life cycle and links efforts among the countries it crosses. Source: BTO and the scientific review; results presented 28 July. In Albania… flamingos at the heart of an environmental case Little Egret over Narta Lagoon, Albania — archival photo, 2015.Photo: Pasztilla (Attila Terbócs) / Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. The image is for site identification and does not document current development works. In a report published by BirdLife International on 7 September, attention returned to protests protecting the Vjosa–Narta area in Albania, after a hundred days of actions known as the “flamingo protests.” According to the organization, the coastal area hosts more than two hundred bird species and lies on a migration route between Africa and Europe. The protests concern works and development projects inside a protected area and the risks they pose to wetlands. BirdLife says the channel linking Narta Lagoon to the sea was closed during the works and then reopened, warning of the effect of disrupting water flow on the lagoon’s balance and birds’ food. The case reveals a basic side of protection: the bird needs a place fit for life when it lands. Source: BirdLife, 7 September 2026. From Croatia to Egypt… interconnected stopovers Ferruginous Duck in Aswan, Egypt — archival photo, 2010. terolinjama / iNaturalist, via Wikimedia Commons — CC0. In a piece published on 26 August, BirdLife chose the Ferruginous Duck (English name as given in the source) to illustrate the importance of connectivity among migration stopovers. It notes that the species is classified as Near Threatened, and that its survival depends on the integrity of wetlands separated by vast distances. The piece highlights the Pokuplje basin in Croatia and Lake Nasser in Egypt as important sites for this species and other waterbirds. It also presents a three-year initiative, supported by a grant of £7.5 million, to protect and restore sites on the African–Eurasian flyway. The lesson of this journey is that protecting one site gains greater value when connected to protecting the other sites the bird needs. Source: BirdLife, 26 August 2026. Regulated hunting… quotas monitored and decisions reviewed On the hunting file, the European Federation for Hunting and Conservation (FACE), which represents hunters’ associations, published its 2026 report on the European Turtle Dove on 18 July. The federation presents the experience of adaptive harvest management: setting quotas, recording birds taken, tracking when the allowed ceiling is reached, and closing the season when it is reached. According to its assessment, turtle dove numbers continue to rise on the western flyway, while the situation remains less positive on the central–eastern flyway. These are results presented by a hunters’ federation and should be read in their specific context; they do not mean every bird species has recovered, nor do they provide a basis for generalizing hunting to other regions. But they put a practical question before the debate: how do we link permission to hunt to data on bird numbers and their capacity to recover, and to a real capacity to monitor? Source: FACE, July 2026 report. What do we take away at Sayd? These developments push us to see the season as an epistemic responsibility as well. Correct species identification, documenting sightings, protecting rest places, and respecting the law are elements that can bring together the responsible hunter, the birdwatcher, the photographer, and the researcher. In our view, success in managing the season is measured by the clarity of its rules, the quality of its information, the effectiveness of their application, and by birds remaining able to continue their journey and return in coming years.

articles.title: Black-necked Grebe
articles.body: Black-necked Grebe Podiceps nigricollis — a diving waterbird with contrasting seasonal plumages Name and classification The Black-necked Grebe, Podiceps nigricollis, belongs to Podicipedidae in the order Podicipediformes. North American references call it Eared Grebe; the Saudi reference also records the Arabic name Ghattas adraʿ. AviList 2026 places it among the grebes, specialised swimming and diving birds. It occurs in parts of Eurasia, Africa and North America, with populations ranging from resident to seasonally migratory. Its principal name describes breeding plumage more closely than the paler appearance familiar during winter. Field identification Breeding birds show a black head and neck, golden tufts behind the red eyes and chestnut flanks. In winter the contrast softens: the cheeks and lower neck become pale beneath a dark cap. The fine, slightly upturned bill and high crown above the eye remain useful features. The sexes have similar plumage; juveniles are closer to the non-breeding appearance before developing the bright adult pattern. Winter Horned Grebe is a frequent confusion species but has a stronger bill and a more sharply defined boundary between dark cap and white cheek. Little Grebe differs in bill structure, head shape and its less extensively white winter appearance. Use the combination rather than one mark. Habitat, food and behaviour It uses lakes, pools and marshes, moving outside the breeding season to larger lakes, brackish or saline waters and sheltered coastal bays. Diving brings aquatic insects and larvae, crustaceans and molluscs, with small fish and other prey taken according to local conditions. Some saline lakes rich in invertebrates attract large gatherings, while other sites hold smaller groups. Its use of salt water does not make it exclusively marine: habitat choice changes through the year with food, breeding and moult. An observer may see a bird disappear underwater and resurface some distance from the point where it dived. Breeding and life cycle Pair displays on the water precede nesting, and many pairs may breed close together. Both adults build a platform of aquatic vegetation anchored among reeds or other emergent plants. The British reference gives a usual clutch of three to four eggs and incubation by both sexes for twenty to twenty-two days. Downy chicks can move and swim early, but adults carry them on their backs and feed them. Parents may divide the brood between them. Leaving the floating nest is therefore distinct from becoming fully grown or capable of flight: young birds continue to depend on parental care during early development. Arab distribution and November The 2026 Lebanese guide classifies it as an uncommon winter visitor and passage migrant on wetlands and the coast; Kuwait’s list gives a similar status. In Oman it is a common winter visitor with breeding documented on limited occasions. The Saudi reference describes scarce winter occurrence and records historical breeding in the south-western highlands; this is different from treating all Saudi birds as resident breeders. Moroccan studies document wintering birds and local breeding populations, while the winter range includes North African coasts. November coverage therefore suits the arrival of winter birds in the Levant and Gulf, alongside important local breeding exceptions. Conservation and responsible observation Its global category is Least Concern, LC. Nevertheless, pollution, habitat loss, altered water levels, disturbance at breeding sites and illegal hunting can affect local populations. Floating nests depend on suitable water and vegetation, and protecting several sites is useful because birds move between them. Watch from shore or a distant fixed position, allowing extra space around nests or chicks. Do not pursue a diving bird by boat: repeated diving can be a response to disturbance rather than a photographic opportunity. Notes on location, date and behaviour help distinguish winter occurrence from local breeding. References AviList Core Team — AviList v2026, 20 October 2026. articles.title: Black Stork
articles.body: Black Stork Ciconia nigra Identity and identification Black Stork Ciconia nigra belongs to Ciconiidae. Glossy black covers most of the body, contrasting with a white belly and adult red bill and legs. Juveniles are duller with less red bills. It flies with its neck extended like White Stork, but shows much less white. It is placed in the order Ciconiiformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour More secretive than White Stork, it uses rivers, pools and wetlands near woodland or quiet sites. Fish, amphibians and other small aquatic prey form its diet. Migrants soar on rising air and stop at wetlands for food and rest. Breeding and parental care A large nest occupies a tree or rock ledge within the breeding range. Usually three to five eggs are incubated by both parents for about 32–38 days. Young reach flight at roughly 63–71 days and receive further care. These general durations do not demonstrate nesting in a passage country. Range and Arab occurrence Migration links Eurasian breeding areas with African wintering grounds. In Lebanon it is a passage migrant, recorded from mid-February to mid-June and mid-August to early November. These records establish neither Lebanese residence nor breeding; other countries require their own status descriptions. Seasonality and observation Early November can coincide with the end of eastern Mediterranean autumn passage. Distinguish high travelling flocks from birds stopping to feed. Counts, direction and time document migration more usefully than closely approaching a resting individual. Ecological role and conservation A network of quiet wetlands supports the migration route. Electrocution, collisions, illegal shooting and degraded water habitats are pressures. Protecting stopovers complements protection of distant nests because the journey depends on multiple habitats. References Ramadan-Jaradi et al. — Updated checklist of the birds of Lebanon, Sandgrouse 42 (2020), 186–238. University of Michigan Museum of Zoology — Animal Diversity Web: Ciconia nigra. AviList Core Team — AviList: The Global Avian Checklist, v2026 (20 October 2026). Photo: Dave Brown — CC0 1.0.

articles.title: Black Wheatear
articles.body: Black Wheatear Oenanthe leucura A rocky-country wheatear of the western Arab world Black Wheatear, Oenanthe leucura, belongs to the flycatcher family Muscicapidae and measures about 18 cm. At a distance it can seem almost uniformly black, until movement over the rocks reveals the white rump and tail. Its Arab distribution is centred on northwestern Africa, unlike White-crowned Wheatear, whose desert range extends much farther east. Geographical context helps identification, but cannot replace examining the bird itself, particularly where the two species may occur together. Its presence in November usually reflects local residency rather than a long seasonal passage. A pair may remain within its territory outside the breeding season, even if singing decreases or the birds use different parts of their habitat. Returning to the same slope on separate days may therefore reveal birds missed on a first visit. Silence is not absence, and a solitary bird is not proof of a migrant newly arrived from the European side of the Mediterranean. Male, female and juvenile plumages Males are very dark, appearing blacker and more lustrous in favourable light, while females tend towards dark brown. Juveniles broadly resemble females but look duller. White on the rump and much of the tail contrasts with black central feathers and a continuous black terminal band, together making an inverted T-like pattern. This becomes clear when the tail spreads and is more dependable than judging gloss from a shaded photograph. A black-headed White-crowned Wheatear can look similar, but normally lacks the same uninterrupted terminal band and differs in the distribution of white and black below. The French name Traquet rieur refers to this same Black Wheatear, not another species. AviList v2026 places the African populations under the subspecies name riggenbachi. Older names occur in earlier guides; they should not be counted as separate species or additional birds in an inventory. Arab countries and the limits of the range The North African resident range includes Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and parts of Libya. More specific Libyan regional accounts place it in the northwest, including Jebel Nafusa, rather than throughout the country. The range has western desert extensions, and AviList's description reaches extreme northwestern Mauritania. These boundaries do not imply uniform abundance. The species may be familiar at a suitable cliff and absent from a large nearby area that lacks comparable structure. Outside the Arab world, populations occur on the Iberian Peninsula, with a limited European distribution compared with the African range. Black Wheatear is not a widespread resident of the Levant or Arabian Peninsula. Gaps in the map should not be filled with expectations based on similar-looking desert scenery. A record far from the usual range requires checking the tail pattern and possible confusion with White-crowned Wheatear before suggesting exceptional movement or range expansion. Rocks, cliffs and winter It favours dry, open ground with slopes, cliffs and rocky ravines, and can use walls, abandoned buildings or stone terraces. It needs exposed areas for finding food alongside crevices and shelter, rather than dense tree cover. Planting more trees is therefore not automatically beneficial if it changes open habitat into cover that obscures the ground. Its needs differ from those of woodland birds, even when all occupy the same geographical region. Although primarily resident, some upland birds may descend during severe cold, and juveniles disperse beyond their birthplace. These movements differ from regular migration between Europe and Africa. Iberian research supports pairs remaining in their territories through winter. That does not mean every Maghreb population behaves identically under all conditions. Distinguishing altitudinal movement, juvenile dispersal and residency helps interpret an unfamiliar autumn record without forcing all three into a single explanation. Catching prey on the ground Most food consists of invertebrates, such as beetles, ants and other insects, with additional prey that may include spiders or small animals. The bird watches from a prominent point before moving onto the ground, searching among stones and across exposed surfaces. Small quantities of fruit and berries may also be eaten in autumn and winter. This variation makes a description based on one food type misleading, but does not turn the species into a bird dependent solely on plants. Natural perches shorten the distance between watching and striking at prey. Raised stones and rocky edges consequently serve a feeding function as well as offering resting places. Watching a bird return to the same perch helps explain its hunting technique, but does not establish the size of its territory. Stones should not be moved or shrubs removed to make a photograph clearer: prey and shelter are part of the landscape on which the bird depends. Stone carrying: construction and a behavioural signal One of this wheatear's best-known behaviours is carrying small stones into cavities near the nesting place. Females transport stones associated with the nest, while males carry larger quantities in displays studied by researchers. Stones can accumulate over successive seasons when a site is reused, so the size of a pile does not represent one day's work or a single breeding attempt. Nor does every cavity containing stones prove that eggs are currently present. Experiments and other studies indicate that male stone carrying has a role in display and communication with the female, rather than serving only to support the nest. A study published in Ibis examined the properties of selected stones and the costs of carrying them at rocky sites and abandoned buildings in southeastern Spain. This does not mean every function of the behaviour has been settled, or that the findings were measured in all Arab populations. In the field, the essential point is to leave these structures intact rather than dismantle them out of curiosity. Breeding and the development of young The nest occupies a rock cavity, wall or suitable building and contains a cup of grasses, roots and soft materials. Spanish studies describe laying mainly in spring, and more than one brood or replacement attempt may occur within a season. A European regional calendar should not be transferred unchanged to every Maghreb locality. References give typical clutches of about 3–6 eggs, with differences between studies. The count in one nest remains a local observation, not a fixed standard for the whole species. The female incubates for roughly two weeks, and both parents feed the chicks. Studies describe young remaining in the nest for about two weeks, followed by at least another two weeks of care after departure in the populations studied. A bird that has begun flying may therefore still be dependent. Predation, habitat and food influence the outcome, and repeated attempts do not guarantee success. This explains why nest counts or food deliveries are not equivalent to the number of young reaching independence. Protection and the value of repeated observation AviList v2026 lists the species as globally Least Concern, LC. Nevertheless, its relatively restricted range, fragmented breeding sites and differing local conditions make cliffs, shelters and open ground important conservation resources. Changes such as construction or altered land use can damage a particular site without changing the global assessment. A healthy population in one country cannot compensate for the loss of a small group in another. Observers can help by recording the date, habitat, number of birds and visible features, then revisiting from a safe distance instead of pressuring birds to appear. Do not inspect nest cavities by hand, collect souvenir stones around them or pursue a young bird for a photograph. Repeated playback near territorial pairs should also be avoided. Observing natural behaviour gives a truer account than a picture obtained through disturbance, and global status is not permission to hunt or alter habitat. Photo: karim Attouche / iNaturalist (CC0 1.0)

articles.title: Austria takes team gold at Cairo’s 300m Rifle World Championship
articles.body: Three rifle shooters take aim from the standing position on a shooting range. Austria leads the men’s prone team event on 18 October, a day after Finland took individual gold and Norway won the team title in three positions. Austria won the men’s 300m prone team gold on Sunday, 18 October 2026, at the World Championship being held at Egypt International Olympic City in the New Administrative Capital. The team scored 1,782 points with 91 inner tens, ahead of Switzerland and Poland. Alexander Schmirl scored 595, Patrick Diem 595 and Andreas Thum 592. Switzerland finished second with 1,780 points and 95 inner tens, and Poland third with 1,777 and 83 inner tens. Egypt placed eighth with 1,719 points and 46 inner tens. Finnish and Norwegian gold in three positions Finland’s Aleksi Leppa had won the men’s individual 300m rifle three positions title on 17 October with 591 points and 29 inner tens. Poland’s Maciej Kowalewicz matched his points total but recorded 22 inner tens to take silver, while Norway’s Jon-Hermann Hegg earned bronze with 589 points and 23 inner tens. In the three positions team event, Norway led with 1,760 points, followed by Austria on 1,753 and Switzerland on 1,751. Egypt finished sixth with 1,673 points. A separate event on Cairo’s calendar The championship runs from 15 to 20 October, bringing together 57 athletes from 19 countries. The programme for 19 October includes the men’s individual prone event and the open standard rifle event. This championship is a separate competition from the Rifle/Pistol World Cup hosted by Cairo earlier in the same month. articles.title: Calandra Lark
articles.body: Calandra Lark Melanocorypha calandra A large lark concealed in the fields The Calandra Lark, Melanocorypha calandra, is a bird of agricultural plains and grassy steppes, not a woodland species despite its elaborate song. A member of the lark family, it measures about 18–20 centimetres. Its body is substantial and its bill strongly conical, while the streaked brown upperparts resemble soil and dry grass stems. A field can consequently appear empty until several birds move together. Vernacular names shared between different larks are not, by themselves, sufficient evidence for identification. Adults have two conspicuous black patches at the sides of the lower neck. The dark underwings are bordered by a striking white trailing edge in flight. Reliable identification combines these marks with bill shape and build rather than relying on breast colour or a local name. The sexes look similar. Young birds can have very weak or absent black patches, together with pale edges to back and wing feathers. Weak neck markings alone do not establish that a bird is female. Separating similar larks The Bimaculated Lark, Melanocorypha bimaculata, also has a heavy bill and paired black neck patches. Calandra, however, shows a strong contrast between its dark underwing and white trailing edge, as well as white on the outermost tail feathers. Bimaculated lacks that broad trailing band, and its shorter-looking tail shows white tips rather than the same pattern. A bird seen only standing and facing the observer may remain unidentified, especially at distance or in harsh light. Eurasian Skylark has a smaller bill and a less substantial build, without the same large paired neck patches. Crested Lark draws attention to its pointed crest and longer bill. Record relative size, bill shape and the wing and tail patterns when birds take off naturally. Chasing a flock to obtain one additional feature is unnecessary: waiting at a field edge often provides a better view while allowing the birds to continue feeding. Habitat, food and daily activity Calandra Larks favour extensive open areas with grassy vegetation, including steppe, rain-fed cereal fields and pasture. Land being undeveloped does not automatically make it suitable: dense trees or tall scrub change its character. An open field can combine ground for walking and searching for food, vegetation that conceals a nest, and shorter patches from which birds can detect danger. The value of these elements changes with the season and the way the land is managed. Food is collected on the ground, with invertebrates becoming particularly important during breeding and chick rearing. In autumn and winter the birds eat seeds and other plant material, including grass leaves and shoots. This seasonal shift explains the importance of crop residues and grassy margins, not merely the grain crop itself. Removing all wild plants and using pesticides intensively can reduce both animal and plant foods. A flock moving among fields depends on a network of habitats rather than one patch that happens to be good on a particular day. Song, pairing and nest construction The male rises in song above the breeding ground, delivering varied phrases that can include imitations of other birds. This display is more than an attractive performance: it contributes to territorial advertisement and communication during pairing. Breeding pairs occupy territories, which may be close together where suitable habitat is concentrated. A winter gathering does not mean that a colony of nests will occupy the same place. European references place breeding mainly between spring and early summer, with timing varying geographically. A Spanish calendar cannot be treated as a fixed schedule for Morocco or Iraq. The nest sits in a small hollow on the ground, sheltered by low vegetation, and its cup is made from stems, grasses and lighter material. The female takes the main role in construction and incubation. Surrounding cover remains important for safety, so opening a route towards a nest can expose its position even without touching it. From eggs to independent birds The Spanish vertebrate encyclopaedia compiles a clutch range of three to six eggs, most often four or five. It gives incubation as generally 11–13 days, sometimes extending to 16 days. These are reference ranges rather than a guaranteed timetable for every nest. Their variation illustrates why the species' life history should not be reduced to one unattributed number, or a hatching date calculated from seeing a sitting bird without knowing when laying began. According to the same reference, chicks remain in the nest for about eight to ten days, then leave while still requiring care. Nest departure does not mean independence or proficient flight. Both parents help feed them, and a failed breeding attempt may be followed by another. After breeding, gatherings and movements become more conspicuous. Protecting a breeding site must include chicks hidden near the nest, not just eggs: cultivation or vehicles can injure young birds invisible to a passer-by. Arab distribution and the November scene The range extends from western Europe and northwestern Africa into western and central Asia. In Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia the species is a resident breeder of suitable plains, while the wider range includes partly migratory populations. Winter movements reach parts of the Mediterranean basin. Consequently, not every individual in an autumn flock need have originated locally, and a photograph alone cannot reveal the country where it hatched. Iraq, Syria and western Jordan lie within its regional Levantine and Middle Eastern range, with differences among habitats and populations. AviList identifies Mediterranean Egypt and Jordan as winter destinations for migrants, alongside Iran outside the Arab world. This does not imply uniform occurrence throughout those countries. In November, open farmland and steppe are useful places to follow gatherings, recording dates, numbers and habitat rather than describing the bird as present everywhere. The Gulf presents a different situation. The Kuwaiti reference describes it as a vagrant, and the regional review documents limited records in Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, including autumn and winter observations. The Saudi reference records its presence at sites in the kingdom without treating it as a common regular winter species. The arrival of a flock at a Gulf farm in one winter neither establishes a breeding habitat nor guarantees its return every year. Conservation and responsible observation AviList 2026 records Calandra Lark as globally Least Concern, LC, but a national assessment can be more worrying: Spain assesses its breeding population as Near Threatened. Different geographical scales do not constitute a contradiction. Agricultural intensification, conversion of steppe to orchards or tree plantations, and the removal of fallow land threaten the diversity of open habitats. Conservation does not always mean planting trees; steppe birds need functioning steppe. Observe from established roads and edges without entering plots where nesting behaviour is evident. Keep dogs and vehicles away from ground cover, and avoid playback or repeatedly making birds fly. Repeated records within the same season help distinguish genuine change from differences in observation effort. Finally, a global conservation category does not grant permission to hunt: local legal frameworks are separate from extinction-risk classification. Photo: karim Attouche / iNaturalist (CC0 1.0)

articles.title: Common Bulbul
articles.body: Common Bulbul Pycnonotus barbatus Identity and identification Common Bulbul Pycnonotus barbatus belongs to Pycnonotidae. Maghreb birds have a dark head, grey-brown body and pale undertail, without a large white cheek or striking white eye-ring. Colour varies across its African range, so southern photographs should not represent every geographical population. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Gardens, orchards, woodland and cultivated edges provide habitat. It eats fruit, insects and other plant material, appearing in pairs or small groups. Algerian diet studies document fruit and invertebrates and links with seasonally changing resources. Breeding and parental care A cup nest is placed in dense vegetation or a suitable tree. Young need provisioning before and after nest departure. Breeding timing varies with region and conditions. Rarely seeing concealed nests does not imply that local birds fail to breed. Range and Arab occurrence Widespread in Africa, it is familiar as a resident in parts of Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia. It should not be equated with White-spectacled Bulbul in the Levant or White-eared Bulbul in Iraq and the Gulf: these are separate species with different marks and ranges. Seasonality and observation November observation is possible in resident Maghreb areas, particularly at fruiting trees. Record undertail colour, head pattern and photograph location. A vernacular record naming only a bulbul cannot establish species without description or a clear image. Ecological role and conservation It disperses some fruit seeds and consumes insects. Scrub clearance, pesticides and bird trade are pressures. Diverse gardens with native fruiting plants preserve food and refuge; concealed nests should remain covered rather than exposed for photography. articles.title: Common Buzzard
articles.body: Common Buzzard Buteo buteo — A broad-winged raptor with variable plumage, soaring over open country and migrating through the Levant Identity and recognition The Common Buzzard, Buteo buteo, is a diurnal raptor of the family Accipitridae. Arabic references also call it al-bazi al-hawwam. Broad wings, a relatively short tail and a substantial body characterize its shape. Individuals range from dark brown to extensively pale plumage, and often soar with their wings in a shallow V. AviList 2026 retains the Steppe Buzzard, Buteo buteo vulpinus, as a subspecies within this species. It is an important migrant through the Levant. Different populations are resident or migrate over varying distances. Age, sex and similar species The sexes look broadly similar, and overall colour alone is unreliable for separating them. Adults generally show a distinct dark terminal tail band and dark trailing edges to the wings; ageing requires several feather characters and their condition. Long-legged Buzzards, Buteo rufinus, differ in structure, proportions and plumage details, but colour overlap can confuse observers. European Honey Buzzards, Pernis apivorus, have a smaller, more projecting head and a relatively longer tail. Views of both wings and tail from several angles improve identification, particularly in mixed gatherings of migrating raptors. Habitat, food and behaviour Open land, pasture and fields adjoining trees or woodland provide suitable habitat. A buzzard may watch the ground from a post or tree, or soar in rising air before descending on prey. Its flexible diet includes rodents and other small mammals, birds, reptiles and invertebrates, as well as carrion. Birds sometimes walk across fields looking for earthworms. Their needs combine accessible feeding ground with elevated resting or nesting sites, explaining frequent appearances beside roads and fields even though cities are not their principal habitat. Breeding and life cycle Buzzards build stick nests within their breeding range, and raising young requires weeks of parental care. British nest records typically indicate one brood of two or three eggs. Incubation lasts approximately 34 days and is mainly performed by the female, sometimes with male participation; young usually fledge at around 44–52 days. These are reference values from British monitoring, with breeding dates varying by population and region. Migratory populations complete their annual cycle between northern nesting areas, passage corridors and southern wintering grounds. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes autumn passage from early August to November and regular wintering by the nominate subspecies from November to mid-March, especially in the Beqaa. Vulpinus passes in larger numbers and winters less regularly. Jordan records common passage by Steppe Buzzards and winter occurrence of the nominate form. Saudi references describe autumn migration particularly in the west during September and October, with limited winter presence in southern Tihama. Egypt includes important Red Sea corridors for Steppe Buzzards; research at Galala Observatory documents the significance of spring passage there. Late October consequently falls near the end of passage and approaching winter residence in parts of the Levant. Ecology and conservation Buzzards consume rodents and other animals; scavenging also returns material to food webs. AviList 2026 lists global Least Concern using Red List data. Local hazards include shooting, poisoning and loss of feeding or nesting sites. Safe migration corridors are particularly important where many raptors concentrate, while monitoring winter sites helps distinguish temporarily settled birds from passing migrants. articles.title: Eurasian Chaffinch
articles.body: Eurasian Chaffinch Fringilla coelebs — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and taxonomy The Eurasian Chaffinch, Fringilla coelebs, also called Common Chaffinch, is a finch approximately 15 cm long. This account follows the modern restricted species concept. African Chaffinch, Fringilla spodiogenys, resident and breeding in the Maghreb, is separate, as are the Atlantic-island species formerly grouped with it. Identification Males have a blue-grey head, pink-brown face and underparts, warm brown back and olive-green rump. Females are quieter grey-brown birds, and juveniles resemble them. Both sexes show conspicuous white wing markings and white outer tail feathers. The conical bill is shorter and stronger than that of a specialist insect-eater. Brambling has a white rump and stronger orange on the shoulders and breast. Separating Eurasian and African Chaffinches, particularly females and incompletely coloured birds, requires a combination of plumage, locality and vocal evidence rather than one isolated feature. Habitat, food and behaviour Breeding habitat includes broadleaved and coniferous woodland, orchards and tree-rich gardens. In winter the species also uses farmland, verges and open ground close to shelter. It eats seeds and invertebrates; insects and larvae become especially important when feeding chicks. Much feeding takes place on the ground, sometimes in mixed flocks with Bramblings and other species. Short, clear calls accompany a repeated song phrase ending in a distinctive flourish. Males defend breeding territories, whereas behaviour becomes more social outside the season. Breeding and life cycle The female constructs a compact cup in a tree or shrub from fine vegetation, fibres and moss, sometimes camouflaging it with lichens. A typical clutch contains 4–5 eggs, incubated by the female for approximately 12–13 days. Both parents provide food, and chicks leave the nest after about a fortnight. Timing varies with place and altitude: documented breeding in Lebanon extends from mid-March to late July. Adequate insect food and protected nest sites matter even for a bird associated with winter seed feeding. Arab distribution and seasons Some southern populations are resident while northern and eastern populations move south and west in autumn. Lebanon supports common resident breeders, joined by passage and winter birds from early October to late April, especially in woodland and orchards. Northern Iraq has limited breeding as well as winter occurrence. Jordan’s Dibbeen woodland supports wintering chaffinches; Egypt also receives winter visitors. Breeding chaffinches in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and much of the Libyan Maghreb belong to the separate African Chaffinch, not automatically to this species. Published records from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates show rare occurrence, a very different situation from Lebanon. Overlap among chaffinch species during the cold season makes careful identification valuable. Ecology and conservation Seed and invertebrate consumption connect the species to food webs in which it also feeds natural predators. Conservation references list Least Concern, although older assessments need their taxonomic scope checked. British declines have been associated with trichomonosis and other factors; the same explanation should not be assumed for every Arab population change. Maintaining trees, hedges and varied food resources, while reducing pesticide pressure, supports its habitats. articles.title: Study: common loons choose breeding lakes that resemble where they hatched
articles.body: A common loon in breeding plumage in Minocqua, Wisconsin, July 2011. An illustrative photograph of the species examined in the study. Data from northern Wisconsin link breeding-territory choice to shoreline development on natal lakes, while revealing a different nest response close to hatching. A bird’s first lake may leave a lasting mark on its choice of the next. That is what a new study of common loons (Gavia immer) in northern Wisconsin suggests: the birds settled to breed in territories resembling their natal lakes in their level of shoreline development. The study was published in Behavioral Ecology on 17 October 2026 as an accepted manuscript, before final copyediting and typesetting. Its authors are Emily Renkey, Katie Adler and Daniel Blumstein of the University of California, Los Angeles, and Walter Piper of Chapman University. The first lake as a reference point The researchers drew on a marked population in a long-term study in northern Wisconsin between 1992 and 2023 to investigate links between shoreline development and human activity, breeding-territory choice and nest-defense behavior. Similarity in shoreline development was one of the striking findings. The researchers interpreted this pattern as an indication of natal habitat imprinting: features of the early environment becoming a reference for later breeding-habitat selection. This means choosing a similar environment, rather than necessarily returning to the same lake. Closer to hatching, less likely to leave In another part of the study, the team found no effect of shoreline development on the distance at which a loon left its nest as humans approached. Incubating birds were, however, less likely to leave the nest late in the incubation period. The researchers view this response as consistent with greater investment in protecting a breeding attempt as hatching approaches. The finding concerns nest-leaving behavior under the study conditions; it does not establish that development or human approaches are harmless to the birds. Are the birds responding to people or to food? The match between natal and breeding lakes does not establish exactly which features the birds recognize. The researchers suggest another possibility: common loons may be seeking lakes with familiar fish-species communities, rather than being attracted by the level of human activity itself. This remains a possible explanation, not a cause demonstrated by the findings. The distinction matters: a bird choosing a lake with familiar features does not mean it prefers buildings or is immune to their effects. Choosing a habitat does not guarantee its safety For conservation context, New Hampshire’s Loon Preservation Committee explains that development along lake shores and islands has reduced nesting habitat on many lakes. People approaching nests can also cause incubating birds to enter the water, leaving their eggs exposed to predators, heat or cold. The Wisconsin study adds a behavioral perspective: the environment in which a bird grew up may influence its later choices, even when that environment includes a human presence. But the research concerns a particular species in a particular region. It is not sufficient to extend the finding to other birds or to wetlands in the Arab region. articles.title: Common Quail — Coturnix coturnix
articles.body: Common quailPhoto: Dûrzan Cîrano — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. Range: A small ground bird of the pheasant family, heard more often than seen. It breeds across Europe, North Africa, and western Asia, and winters in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of southern Asia. Lebanon and the Levant form a key autumn and spring passage corridor; it hides in cereal fields, pastures, and dense grass, and rarely flies except in short low bursts before dropping back into cover. Life cycle and habitat: Males usually reach breeding grounds ahead of females. The female scrapes a shallow nest on the ground, lined with a little plant material, and typically lays between 8 and 13 eggs, incubating them alone for about 17–20 days. The chicks are precocial: they leave the nest soon after hatching and feed themselves, with the mother brooding them in the first weeks. Plumage is nearly complete by about day 19. It prefers open habitats with enough grass cover to hide in, and avoids dense forest; its diet is grass seeds, fallen grain, and insects and their larvae. Lifestyle: Secretive and terrestrial; it creeps more than it flies. The male’s short, repeated call is heard at dawn and dusk—and sometimes at night—while the bird itself stays hidden among the stalks. Much of the migration is nocturnal. Its wings are relatively longer than those of many ground gamebirds, matching a true long-distance migrant rather than a local wanderer. Outside the breeding season it may gather in small groups on passage or in winter. It should not be confused with the Japanese quail Coturnix japonica despite superficial likeness; each has a distinct call and core range. Common quailPhoto: LuisNDamas — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. Hunting status: Across Arab countries, hunting common quail is generally prohibited unless a specific state issues an official seasonal decree that expressly lists it. In Lebanon, Wild Hunting Law No. 580/2004 limits hunting to quarry species set by the minister; everything else is protected year-round; common quail is not among the permitted quarry in the absence of a current open-season decision. Conservation status: Globally Least Concern with the International Union for Conservation of Nature. In Europe it is assessed regionally nearer Near Threatened because of declines linked to intensive farming and hunting on flyways—a regional context, not a substitute for the global listing. Traits: A bird “heard, not seen”: the male announces himself with a short call while remaining hidden. A familiar marker of Levantine fields in migration season, and sensitive to how seasons and farmland habitats are managed.

articles.title: Common Sandpiper in the Arab world: a traveller along the water’s edge
articles.body: Common Sandpiper On a riverside stone or the edge of a pond, a brown-and-white bird takes short steps and teeters before continuing to feed. It may look solitary, well away from large wader flocks. Yet the Common Sandpiper belongs to a broad network of waterways and migration stopovers stretching across the Arab world. Identification card Arabic names: الطيطوي الشائع; الطيطوي الاعتيادي English name: Common Sandpiper French name: Chevalier guignette Scientific name: Actitis hypoleucos Family: Scolopacidae Length: approximately 19–21 cm Habitat: freshwater and saltwater margins, muddy and rocky banks, lakeshores and canals Arab-world occurrence: passage migrant and winter visitor in varying numbers; a summer sighting alone does not establish breeding Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC) Where it occurs in the Arab world National studies in Morocco document wintering birds on both Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts and at inland waters. Tracking of some Scottish breeders has also revealed Moroccan staging sites on journeys to and from West Africa. The country can therefore serve two different purposes: a stopover for some individuals and a wintering area for others. In Lebanon, a wader study published in the Lebanese Science Journal describes a common passage migrant and scarce winter visitor, recorded throughout the year at inland waters, along the coast and on islands. Year-round records do not establish nesting at all those sites: non-breeding birds may remain away from breeding areas. In Saudi Arabia, Common Sandpipers occur on passage and in winter, including inland. Observations also show variation within the country: passage is prominent in the Eastern Province, while smaller numbers winter along its coast and pools. A waterbird is not necessarily confined to the sea or to large marshes. A migration that starts before autumn feels close Post-breeding movement in European populations begins in July, with adults generally preceding juveniles. Many birds reach African wintering areas by October. Riyadh-region records place the main autumn passage between July and late October, with spring movement from March to May. Timing and numbers vary by site, population and year. The first birds may consequently appear in late summer, before the weather suggests autumn. Repeated sightings of one sandpiper do not prove that the same individual has remained: different birds may use the same suitable patch. Dates, counts and behaviour help turn impressions into seasonal observations that can be compared. A white wedge in front of the wing Grey-brown upperparts contrast with a white belly and a white projection rising between the side of the breast and the folded wing. This is particularly useful when comparing it with Green or Wood Sandpipers, which lack the same white shoulder wedge. Its tail extends beyond the folded wings, and the legs look short beside those of many other waders. A white wing-bar shows in flight, often low over water with distinctive flicking wingbeats. There is no reason to flush the bird to see it. Head-bobbing and teetering are frequent while it walks, and may intensify when a person approaches. If it stops feeding and continually watches you, step back. The sexes look similar overall. Feather-edge details differ between juveniles and adults, but ageing requires a clear view and assessable plumage. The strength of a brown tone, or apparent size in an unscaled photograph, cannot establish age or sex confidently. What the bank provides It feeds on aquatic and terrestrial insects and larvae, worms, small crustaceans and molluscs, picking food from the ground and water's edge. It may use a canal bank or small pond that people barely notice. The value lies in food, water and accessible margins, rather than the size or fame of the landscape. It breeds mainly across Europe and Asia, placing the nest near water in concealing vegetation. BTO data give a typical clutch of four eggs, incubated by both sexes. These are facts about the species' biology, not evidence of breeding at an Arab site without a documented nest or confirmed breeding behaviour. Keeping quiet margins available The global category remains Least Concern, but feeding and resting sites matter to successful migration. Loss or pollution of natural banks, and repeated disturbance, can reduce the usefulness of a place that looks small on a map. Watch from a distance. Avoid walking directly towards the bird along a narrow bank or trapping it between yourself and the water. Do not catch it for identification. Check legal status with the competent authority in each country: neither its name nor its conservation category authorises hunting. A clear side-on photograph with a date and location is more useful than a flight image obtained by disturbance. articles.title: Egypt–UAE cooperation to protect houbara and strengthen Omayed Reserve
articles.body: African houbara (Chlamydotis undulata) in Algeria, 2 October 2020. A planned scientific study will support management and habitat conservation in Matrouh, building on cooperation that included African houbara reintroduction in 2022. Egypt and the United Arab Emirates have discussed strengthening cooperation to protect African houbara and improve the management of Omayed Reserve in Matrouh Governorate, through a scientific assessment of the reserve’s ecological characteristics and natural habitats and more coordinated biodiversity protection measures. According to a statement published by Egypt’s Ministry of Local Development and Environment on 18 October 2026, discussions with the UAE-based International Fund for Houbara Conservation covered support for the reserve, protection of its resources and the use of specialist scientific expertise in wildlife management. A scientific assessment of habitats The latest step includes a directive to establish a scientific committee bringing together experts from outside the ministry and representatives of the protected areas sector. The committee will study Omayed’s ecological features, assess its biodiversity and propose appropriate measures to protect its natural resources and habitats. The work focuses on the needs of the reserve and the birds that depend on it, alongside environmental safeguards suited to its characteristics and the long-term health of its ecosystems. The statement did not specify a completion date for the study. Building on the 2022 reintroduction The cooperation builds on an earlier initiative at Omayed on 18 June 2022, when 2,000 African houbara were released and reintroduced. DNA and molecular biology analyses preceded the operation, with results compared against reference samples to confirm that the birds belonged to the local lineage present, or historically present, in Egypt. The cooperation framework also covered joint research and activities to restore and conserve houbara, the exchange of expertise and the development of national wildlife management capacity. It included exploring projects that could deliver economic and social benefits to communities around species conservation areas. A reserve with varied habitats UNESCO has listed Omayed as a biosphere reserve since 1981. The reserve represents part of Egypt’s Mediterranean coastal desert and contains coastal dunes, inland ridges, saline and non-saline depressions, and an inland plateau. According to UNESCO, environmental pressures in the area include land degradation, habitat fragmentation, overgrazing and biodiversity loss. The reserve also has an important role in long-term ecological monitoring, improved rangeland and ecotourism management, and linking nature conservation with sustainable local livelihoods. articles.title: Common Blackbird
articles.body: Common Blackbird Turdus merula — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and identification The Common Blackbird, Turdus merula, is a thrush approximately 24–25 cm long. Adult males are black, usually with a yellow or orange bill and yellow eye-ring. Females are brown with a paler throat and subdued breast markings. Juveniles are brown and mottled: brown plumage alone does not identify a female. Young males may retain dark bills and relatively brown wings. Compared with a starling, the tail is long. On the ground, hopping or short runs alternate with pauses. Similar species and taxonomy Ring Ouzel generally shows a pale breast crescent and feather edges that make its wings appear paler; immature birds with a weak crescent need care. Starlings have shorter tails and pointed wings. This account includes North African blackbirds within Turdus merula rather than converting subspecies differences into separate species. The Indian, Tibetan and Chinese Blackbirds separated by modern taxonomies are excluded. Habitat, diet and voice Woodland, scrub, orchards, gardens and urban green spaces are suitable where ground-feeding opportunities and nearby cover coexist. Blackbirds turn leaves and search soil for earthworms, insects and other invertebrates, adding fruit when available. Diet varies with season, habitat and soil moisture. Rich, fluting song is often delivered from an elevated perch; sharp alarm calls sound very different. Breeding birds defend territories, whereas several may gather at a fruit source without forming a nesting colony. Breeding and life cycle The female builds a substantial cup of plant material strengthened with mud and lined with finer material, in a bush, tree or sheltered position. A typical clutch contains 3–4 eggs, with variation, and incubation lasts roughly 12–14 days. Both parents feed chicks, which leave the nest after about two weeks. Multiple broods are possible, and parental care continues after fledging. A Moroccan study documented breeding in apple orchards and adjacent woody vegetation at Ait Ayach. Such local work illustrates why breeding calendars should be related to habitat rather than copied automatically from European accounts. Arab distribution and seasons Blackbirds are not merely Arab-region winter visitors. Resident breeding populations occur in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, and in parts of the Levant and northern Iraq. In Lebanon the species is a common resident, supplemented by smaller numbers of passage and winter birds between mid-October and mid-March. Jordan illustrates an altitudinal contrast: Wadi Faynan receives winter visitors, whereas higher Wadi Dana supports residents. Breeding has also been recorded in Egyptian oases, so Egypt cannot be described solely as a migration destination. Qatar records are rare, unlike the situation in Mediterranean resident areas. Globally, some northern populations move south in autumn while others remain, and migrants may join places already occupied by local blackbirds. Ecology and conservation Blackbirds consume invertebrates, disperse seeds of some fruits and provide food for raptors and other predators. Their global category is Least Concern, but local trends differ. Pressures include hedge and ground-cover removal, pesticides, collisions and cat predation. Retaining dense shrubs and safe leaf litter and avoiding nest disturbance supports the species. Success in some cities does not mean every population is insensitive to habitat change. articles.title: Eurasian Coot: resident and migrant flocks meet in Arab wetlands
articles.body: Eurasian Coot From a distance it looks like an unassuming dark waterbird. Closer views reveal two prominent features: a white bill and a white shield on the forehead. The Eurasian Coot combines diving skills with life in winter flocks. Yet not every coot seen in October is a new arrival: at some Arab wetlands, resident breeding birds meet visitors from colder regions. Identification card Arabic name: الغرّة الأوراسية; the Saudi bird reference uses غراء أوراسية. English: Eurasian Coot; French: Foulque macroule. Scientific name: Fulica atra, family Rallidae, order Gruiformes. Despite sharing the water with ducks, it is not a duck. Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC), which does not mean every local population is stable. The scientific name follows AviList v2026; regional references document differing patterns of occurrence between countries. [1] [2] [7] Why watch it in autumn? European ringing data show autumn movements beginning in late August and strengthening from mid-September, with returns to distant wintering sites during October. They also document connections between south-western Europe and North Africa. These are observed migration patterns, not a common arrival calendar for all Arab coots: the species includes both resident and migratory populations. [11] An Arab map of residence, passage and wintering Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes the coot as a resident breeder at inland wetlands, and very common on passage and in winter, mainly from September to late May. Seeing a bird in autumn therefore does not establish that it is a migrant; nor does a winter flock show that all its members breed at that site. [3] In Morocco, a study of Daya Takaddoum in the Bouregreg valley documented breeding in 2018 and 2019, and increasing numbers with the arrival of winter visitors. This is local field evidence, not a current nationwide count. Tunisian winter surveys conducted in 2020–2021 and published in 2024 also recorded the species, underlining the seasonal importance of wetlands. [4] [6] Saudi Arabia’s bird reference classifies it as a rare breeding resident and an uncommon winter visitor, occurring in winter from October to March. The Emirates Bird Records Committee checklist, updated in February 2026, calls it a locally common migrant and winter visitor, with resident breeding populations at particular sites, including Al Warsan Lakes and Al Wathba Wetland Reserve. Such differences rule out treating one country’s status as that of the entire Gulf. [2] [5] In Egypt, the Lake Burullus Key Biodiversity Area account, whose latest listed assessment is from 2016, includes coots among wintering waterbirds. This is reference evidence of the site’s winter importance, not a recent count. [12] In Iraq’s Central Marsh, a study published in 2017 recorded coots as winter visitors from November to March during surveys conducted from October 2013 to June 2014. It did not record them in the breeding season within the study area; this does not establish an absence of breeding throughout Iraq. [13] Recognising age and distinguishing similar species Adult coots have charcoal-grey bodies, blacker heads and white bills and frontal shields. Their long toes carry separate skin lobes that aid swimming, unlike the continuous webbing familiar in ducks. To take off, they run across the water before gaining height. [8] The sexes look similar: black plumage alone does not identify an individual’s sex. Juveniles are paler, with greyish white on the face, fore-neck and breast, and a frontal shield that is not yet fully developed. The Red-knobbed Coot Fulica cristata is particularly similar. Red knobs above the shield help identify breeding adults, but their apparent absence in a distant photograph is not enough to exclude that species. [9] Adult Common Moorhens Gallinula chloropus, by contrast, have a red frontal shield. Combine head, bill and body shape rather than calling every dark waterbird a coot. [8] Food, habitat and behaviour Coots use lakes, ponds and slow-flowing waterways, including urban waters. They eat aquatic plants and seeds, as well as molluscs, insects and larvae, diving for food or grazing close to the bank. Their presence in a treatment pond does not make its water drinkable, and bird abundance alone is not a water-quality test. [10] Life cycle: from nest to flock Both partners build a nest of plant material near aquatic cover, share incubation and care for the young, and defend the surrounding territory. Breeding-season disputes between neighbours can be fierce, unlike the winter gatherings that bring many individuals together. [2] [8] BTO data give a typical clutch of 5–7 eggs, incubation of about 21–24 days and flight capability at roughly 55–60 days. The downy young can move early but remain dependent on parental care. These are reference values, not fixed numbers or durations for every Arab nest; a European nesting calendar cannot simply be transferred to a different climate. [7] Its value, and what needs protecting Following coots helps reveal how a lake is used throughout the year: where flocks feed, and where vegetation suitable for nesting remains. The Daya Takaddoum study highlights wetland habitat change under urban pressure. Protecting the place, not just the bird, preserves opportunities to feed, breed and rest. [4] Watch from the bank without repeatedly forcing birds to flee, and do not approach nests or chicks for a better photograph. Record the date, site, count and behaviour, distinguishing a sighting from breeding evidence. Global Least Concern status neither automatically permits hunting nor replaces local regulations. articles.title: Eurasian Jay
articles.body: Eurasian Jay Garrulus glandarius Identity and identification Eurasian Jay Garrulus glandarius belongs to Corvidae. A pinkish-brown body, blue-and-black wing panel, dark moustache and white rump in flight are useful features. Head pattern varies geographically. The sexes look alike; the blue panel should be read with shape and other markings. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. Habitat, food and behaviour Woodland, forest and wooded orchards, especially with oaks, provide habitat. It eats acorns, seeds, insects and other animal food and caches supplies in the ground. Harsh calls often reveal it before a view, and mimicry occurs. Acorns are important but not its only food. Breeding and parental care A twig cup is built in a tree. References commonly give four or five eggs, incubation around 18 days and nest departure about 20–23 days after hatching. Both parents care for young and continue feeding after departure. Climate and altitude influence the calendar. Range and Arab occurrence Widespread through Eurasian woodland, it also occurs in North African and Levantine forests. Lebanon’s checklist describes an abundant breeding resident in wooded habitats. This does not extend its ecological requirements to open Arab deserts. Seasonality and observation Resident populations can be observed year-round. Autumn collection and storage reveal acorn transport. November woodland-edge viewpoints allow watching without interrupting journeys to caches. Ecological role and conservation Some unrecovered cached acorns germinate, contributing to tree dispersal. Forest loss and fragmentation reduce habitat. Protecting connected oak woods benefits both jays and woodland regeneration, without reducing a varied animal to a single role or calling it harmful for occasionally taking prey. articles.title: Eurasian Nuthatch
articles.body: Eurasian Nuthatch Sitta europaea Identity and names A compact bird moving headfirst down a trunk offers an excellent introduction to the Eurasian Nuthatch, Sitta europaea. It belongs to Sittidae within the passerines, and is called Sittelle torchepot in French and خازن البندق الأوراسي in Arabic; the Lebanese guide also uses the Arabic name كاسر الجوز الأوروبي. At approximately 14 cm long, with a wingspan around 24 cm, it is small enough to disappear behind a branch. Its powerful bill and short tail give it a distinctive outline. Identification The upperparts are blue-grey, with a dark line passing through the eye and pale cheeks and throat. Underparts vary geographically from whitish to buff, with warmer chestnut on the flanks and beneath the tail; males often have richer flank colour. Colour alone is therefore a poor guide to sex or subspecies. Treecreepers are browner and finely patterned above, with slender curved bills. Western Rock Nuthatch, Sitta neumayer, is a different species: compare the tail, underparts and habitat rather than relying on the shared dark eye-stripe. Habitat and food Mature woodland offers both feeding surfaces and nesting cavities. Deciduous and mixed woods, wooded parks and old orchards can be suitable where large trees remain. The bird searches bark and branches for insects, larvae and spiders, using its feet to move in different directions. Seeds and nuts become particularly important outside the breeding season. Hard items can be wedged in a crevice and hammered open, while food is also cached. This seasonal flexibility helps explain its generally resident way of life. Range and Arab occurrence Its range spans much of temperate Eurasia and reaches Morocco, where resident occurrence is recorded in the global assessment. Arab occurrence is nevertheless localized, not a continuous belt across North Africa and Arabia. The 2026 Birds of Lebanon guide describes a very rare, localized breeding resident in woodland and forest. That is quite different from its account of the widespread Western Rock Nuthatch. A familiar nuthatch seen on a Lebanese cliff should consequently not be assigned to Sitta europaea merely because it has a blue-grey back. Breeding and development The nest occupies an existing cavity, often a natural tree hole or an old woodpecker excavation. The female can narrow the entrance with mud and lay bark fragments inside. BTO gives a typical clutch of 6–8 eggs, female incubation of 16–17 days and a nestling period of roughly 24–25 days. Both parents feed the young. These are useful developmental references, not a Lebanese breeding calendar. Leaving the cavity is a stage in development and should not automatically be interpreted as complete independence. November and responsible observation November is a good time to watch how woodland birds handle and store seeds. A resident encountered then need not have just arrived on migration. Remain on existing paths, allow the bird to move between trees and record habitat as well as plumage. A photograph showing the tail and flanks is more informative than a distant silhouette. Do not open cavities, remove bark or disturb a cache to obtain a closer view. Repeated visits made quietly can reveal more than pursuit of a single individual. Conservation The species is globally Least Concern, a category that does not describe the security of every small population. Retaining mature trees, natural cavities and connected woodland protects its essential resources. The Lebanese guide identifies habitat loss, degradation, disturbance and climate change as pressures. A global range extending across continents cannot compensate for the disappearance of an isolated local wood. Management should retain safe old trees and varied woodland structure rather than treating every dead branch or hollow trunk as material to remove. articles.title: Eurasian Sparrowhawk
articles.body: Eurasian Sparrowhawk Accipiter nisus — An agile bird hunter alternating wingbeats and glides, with females markedly larger than males Identity and recognition The Eurasian Sparrowhawk, Accipiter nisus, is a raptor of the family Accipitridae; AviList 2026 retains this scientific name. Arabic references also call it bashiq al-asafir. A fast predator specializing chiefly in birds, it has relatively short, broad wings and a long, nearly square-ended tail that aid manoeuvring among trees. Rapid wingbeats alternate with brief glides, contrasting with a buzzard’s prolonged soaring. Its populations extend from Europe and northwestern Africa across much of Asia, with northern birds migrating south. Age, sex and similar species Females are substantially larger than males, an important distinction when interpreting prey size and apparent body size. Adult males have blue-grey upperparts and pale underparts barred orange-brown; females are generally brown-grey above with darker barring below. Juveniles are brown above, with differing lower-body markings and sometimes a clear pale eyebrow. Confusion can arise with Levant Sparrowhawks or larger goshawks; body, tail and wing proportions and underwing detail are useful comparisons. Pale eyes and legs and a long tail assist identification, but a combination of features is more reliable than size alone. Habitat, food and behaviour Woodland, forest edges, gardens and tree-rich farmland provide habitat, with cover allowing a concealed approach. The bird flies low beside bushes or buildings before suddenly striking, sometimes pursuing prey into open ground. Small and medium-sized birds form almost its entire diet; smaller males generally take smaller prey than females. Captures may be plucked in a sheltered place. Concentrations of small birds attract sparrowhawks to gardens, where alarm calls may precede the raptor’s appearance. This is part of the natural predator–prey network in such habitats. Breeding and life cycle A stick nest is built in a tree within suitable breeding habitat. British nest records typically indicate one brood of four or five eggs, female incubation lasting approximately 33 days, and fledging at roughly 27–31 days after hatching. These are reference values that vary with conditions and population. Nestlings depend on food supplied by their parents, linking habitat quality to sheltered trees and accessible prey. Migratory individuals use winter grounds separate from their nesting range. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist records common passage from September to early November and March to early May, with small wintering numbers in mountains and the Beqaa from November to late February. Jordan’s list combines common passage and wintering with local residence. Saudi references describe uncommon but widespread passage in September–October and March–April, and winter presence from November to February. In Kuwait it is an uncommon passage migrant and winter visitor associated with suitable wooded sites. Northwestern Africa also supports the subspecies punicus from Morocco to Tunisia, according to AviList. Late October thus falls within passage and the approach of wintering in the Levant and Gulf, alongside differing resident populations. Ecology and conservation Sparrowhawk research illuminates relationships between raptors, prey and contaminants moving through food chains. British studies documented historical decline caused by organochlorine pesticides that thinned eggshells, followed by recovery as their use diminished. Kuwait’s reference identifies indiscriminate shooting as a local threat. AviList 2026 records global Least Concern, while local population health requires its own monitoring. Protecting trees and movement routes and reducing exposure to poisons helps retain this predator within its natural system.
