articles.title: Eurasian Tree Sparrow
articles.body: Eurasian Tree Sparrow Passer montanus Identity and names Eurasian Tree Sparrow, Passer montanus, is Moineau friquet in French and belongs to Passeridae within the order Passeriformes. It is approximately 14 cm long and usually weighs around 20–24 g. Its name does not confine it to closed forest: trees with cavities, fields and villages may together provide its requirements. It is unrelated at genus level to the American Tree Sparrow, and a sparrow perched in a tree is not necessarily this species. Identification Look for a fully chestnut crown and an isolated black spot on each white cheek, combined with a small black throat patch and an incomplete white collar. The brown back is streaked and the wings have pale bars. Males and females look alike, unlike the strongly different sexes of House Sparrow. Juveniles have a less contrasting face. Male Spanish Sparrows also have chestnut crowns, but lack the isolated cheek spot and show heavier black markings below. Habitat, food and behaviour Farmland edges, orchards and open woodland provide food, shelter and potential nest cavities. Adults eat seeds and grain and also collect insects and other invertebrates, particularly for their chicks. Its relationship with settlements varies geographically: a predominantly rural bird in much of Europe, it readily occupies towns in eastern Asia. Outside breeding, birds may join mixed flocks. Checking individuals rather than labelling an entire flock as ordinary sparrows is therefore a useful identification habit. Range and Arab occurrence Although widespread across Eurasia, its Arab occurrence is limited. The specialist Iraqi checklist describes a rare winter visitor to northern and central Iraq. Lebanon’s 2026 guide treats it as a vagrant, with an uncertain old Litani Valley record and two birds recorded at Qaa in November 2018. The published Oman list classifies it as a vagrant with one record. These situations are not regular residence or breeding and cannot be extended to the Gulf or Maghreb generally. Breeding and development Nests occupy cavities in trees or buildings; suitable nest boxes may also be used. Plant material and feathers line the nest. BTO reports a usual clutch of 5–6 eggs, incubation by both sexes lasting 12–13 days, and young leaving after roughly 15–18 days. These are approximate development periods, not an Arab breeding calendar. A bird standing beside a hole does not establish nesting, and departure from the nest does not necessarily mean immediate independence from parental care. November and responsible observation A possible November observation in Iraq or the Levant deserves careful documentation. Record country, site, date and numbers, seeking a side view of the cheek and a view of the crown without moving after the bird. Shade can conceal the cheek spot, so an uncertain identification is preferable to certainty based on a chestnut crown alone. Allow feeding flocks to continue undisturbed and avoid flushing them towards traffic or repeatedly interrupting access to shelter. Conservation Its global IUCN category is Least Concern, but local declines remain important: Britain experienced a severe historical decrease whose effects persist. Retaining winter seed, insects and nesting cavities in farmland helps meet different seasonal needs. Reducing pesticide pressure and keeping suitable old trees can protect these resources. Where this sparrow is rare, a photograph of a living bird is more valuable than capturing or killing one to establish identity. Local wildlife laws apply regardless of global category. articles.title: Eurasian Wren
articles.body: Eurasian Wren Nannus troglodytes Identity and identification Eurasian Wren Nannus troglodytes belongs to Troglodytidae and is widely recorded under Troglodytes troglodytes. Tiny, brown and barred, it has a pale eyebrow and a short tail often held upright. The sexes look alike and the song is remarkably powerful. Different genus names do not create two species. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Dense scrub, damp woodland, stream margins and gardens with undergrowth provide habitat. It searches leaves and roots for insects, spiders and small invertebrates. Movement is often near the ground; a singing bird need not be visible on an exposed high branch. Breeding and parental care The male builds several domed nests with side entrances; the female selects and lines one. BTO gives five or six eggs, incubated by the female for about 16–18 days. Young leave at roughly 15–18 days and receive further care. These reference durations do not transfer a British calendar to Arab climates. Range and Arab occurrence Widespread in Eurasia, it also occurs in North African and Levantine woodland. Lebanon has common breeding residents in dense, moist habitats from coast to mountains. Neither small size nor song makes every little brown regional bird a wren. Seasonality and observation Resident sites support year-round observation, including November. Calls and watching cover edges are more useful than penetrating dense vegetation. Archive records using old and new names must be reconciled to the same scientific identity. Ecological role and conservation Its invertebrate diet links it to ground cover and local moisture. Leaf-litter removal, scrub clearance and stream drying reduce refuges. Retaining dense vegetated corners in gardens and woods preserves food and nests rather than exposing every ground surface. articles.title: European Red-rumped Swallow
articles.body: European Red-rumped Swallow Cecropis rufula Identity and identification European Red-rumped Swallow Cecropis rufula belongs to Hirundinidae. A rufous rump and nape accompany pale underparts and a long forked tail. Rump, nape and nest structure distinguish it from Barn Swallow. It was separated from Eastern Red-rumped Swallow Cecropis daurica; old records require geographic and taxonomic interpretation. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. Habitat, food and behaviour It catches flying insects over farmland, valleys and open country, sometimes joining other swallows near water. Buildings, bridges and cliffs provide nest sites. Mud and nearby food are complementary resources; a bridge alone does not ensure a colony. Breeding and parental care The enclosed mud nest has a tubular entrance, resembling a flask attached beneath shelter. The pair builds and tends young, provisioning insects. An intact nest can retain value in later seasons. Occupancy must be checked before maintenance work. Range and Arab occurrence Its range includes southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, extending east into Asia. Lebanon’s checklist uses rufula for an uncommon migrant breeder and passage migrant. BTO confirms its separation from the eastern species; historical names must not be counted as additional species. Seasonality and observation Lebanese breeding extends from March to August, with passage mainly in March–April and September–October. November follows most usual local occurrence, while seasonality differs elsewhere. Document rump, nape and tail rather than general colour in flight. Ecological role and conservation It consumes aerial insects and is affected by their decline and nest destruction during bridge or building maintenance. Retaining sound nests, delaying work around occupied ones and reducing pesticides help. Observe entrances at a distance without obstructing parents. articles.title: European Shag
articles.body: European Shag Gulosus aristotelis A diver of rocky coasts The European Shag, Gulosus aristotelis, belongs to the cormorant family and is closely associated with rocky shores and islands rather than inland lakes. Measuring 65–80 centimetres, it has an elongated body, slender neck, conspicuous tail and narrow, hook-tipped bill. Adults can look black at a distance, but good light reveals a green sheen. This is a species in its own right, not simply a small Great Cormorant. Older references call it Phalacrocorax aristotelis. Its populations include Atlantic and Mediterranean forms; the subspecies desmarestii inhabits the Mediterranean and Black Seas. Geography therefore matters when comparing photographs and breeding calendars. A bird photographed beside the North Atlantic does not necessarily represent the appearance or seasonal timing of every Mediterranean shag. Age, sex and the seasonal crest An adult has a dark neck, green eye and a small yellow area at the gape. During courtship, its plumage becomes glossier and a curved tuft develops on the forehead. The crest is seasonal, not a feature required at every sighting. Males and females have similar plumage, although males average larger. Apparent size in a single photograph is insufficient to establish sex. Young birds differ from adults in their brown upperparts and paler underparts. Juvenile Mediterranean birds can have very pale bellies and pale-edged wing coverts. A pale belly does not identify a female, nor does brown plumage automatically indicate another species. Age, lighting and wet feathers all alter appearance, making the shape of the head and bill as important as colour. Separating it from Great Cormorant Great Cormorant, Phalacrocorax carbo, is generally more heavily built, with a larger head, heavier bill and broader neck. European Shag has a steeper forehead, a finer bill and only a small yellow gape area. Adult Great Cormorants show more obvious white around the throat and face and may carry a white thigh patch in breeding plumage. Several features together provide a safer identification than one alone. Juveniles are harder to separate because both species may have pale bellies. Study the head in profile, the thickness of the bill relative to the head and the bird’s shape when it takes off naturally. A marine rock is not conclusive evidence, since Great Cormorants also use coasts. Recording a distant bird as an unidentified cormorant is preferable to certainty unsupported by the view. Food and daily habitat The shag pursues fish by diving from the sea surface, usually in coastal waters over rocky or sandy bottoms. Prey varies geographically and seasonally and includes bottom-associated fish as well as schooling species. Birds may feed alone or in groups. Water alone does not make a suitable habitat: access to food and secure resting places both matter. Between diving trips, birds rest on rocks and may spread their wings. These intervals should not be interrupted by repeated approaches from boats or visitors. Some Mediterranean feeding areas are associated with seabed habitats such as seagrass meadows. Protecting a shag colony consequently involves the surrounding feeding waters, not simply leaving one nesting cliff undeveloped. Nests, eggs and dependent chicks Shags nest in crevices, caves and rocky ledges, often in colonies. The male selects a site and makes head and neck displays during courtship. Nests include materials such as seaweed and twigs, and both partners contribute to parental care. The season begins at different times among regions and years. Mediterranean birds may prepare to breed before winter rather than waiting for spring. A typical clutch contains about three eggs. Both parents incubate for approximately a month, and the chicks hatch naked and helpless. British Trust for Ornithology data give a usual fledging interval of 48–58 days after hatching, a reference range rather than a fixed timetable for every Arab colony. Leaving the nest does not make a youngster safe to approach: developing flight and diving skills remain vulnerable to disturbance. Arab distribution and the November scene The Atlantic range reaches Morocco, while Mediterranean colonies occur in Algeria, Tunisia and Libya. Libya’s wintering-waterbird atlas documents island breeding rather than treating the species as widespread across all wetlands. The same reference describes occurrence on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast as accidental or possibly a rare winter visit, not common nationwide residency. Many populations are resident or make limited movements, but residency does not mean that every bird occupies the same rock throughout the year. The Mediterranean Science Commission’s guide places the beginning of laying in late November at some sites, with considerable variation and breeding continuing into later months. November can therefore bring dispersed birds, returns to colonies and early breeding activity, rather than simply the arrival of winter visitors. Conservation and responsible observation European Shag is globally classified as Least Concern, LC, but this does not exclude local declines. Threats include accidental capture in fishing gear, oil pollution, disturbance of colonies and coastal development. Prolonged storms and reduced prey availability can also make feeding difficult. A species-wide category and the prospects of a small colony vulnerable to losing its nesting site describe different scales. Watch from a distance that allows birds to rest and continue normal behaviour. Avoid landing on breeding islands or taking boats into nesting caves. Useful records include date, numbers, approximate age classes and sea conditions, without turning precise nest locations into crowded destinations. An extinction-risk category is not permission to hunt; reserve restrictions and local rules remain separate obligations. articles.title: France raises bird flu risk after cases increase in neighbouring countries
articles.body: A Eurasian teal at Le Teich bird reserve in France. Archive photograph. Moderate risk level takes effect with additional prevention measures and rules affecting waterfowl hunting France raised its highly pathogenic avian influenza risk level from “negligible” to “moderate” across metropolitan France from 5 November 2026, following an increase in cases recorded in wild birds in several neighbouring countries. The decision reflects the spread of infection along migration routes and the possibility of the virus being carried by migratory birds passing through France. The order was issued on 2 November and published in the Official Journal on 4 November, taking effect the following day. The higher risk level activates additional surveillance and prevention measures, including rules affecting waterfowl hunting. During transport, live decoy birds from different holding sites must not be mixed. Direct contact between decoys resident at a hunting site and those transported to it is also prohibited. In designated special-risk areas, additional restrictions apply to the transport and use of these birds according to their keeper’s category, alongside measures protecting poultry and other captive birds from contact with wild birds. Movements of game birds in these areas are subject to veterinary conditions, with additional virological testing when birds of the duck family are moved between game-bird farms. The measure aims to limit transmission from wild birds to birds kept by people, with stricter local measures possible according to the risk assessment. Source: France’s Official Journal. articles.title: Great Crested Grebe
articles.body: Great Crested Grebe Podiceps cristatus — A lake diver combining local breeding and winter visits Identity and identification Great Crested Grebe, Podiceps cristatus, belongs to Podicipedidae within Podicipediformes, not to the duck family despite sharing many lakes with ducks. AviList 2026 retains this scientific name. It sits low in the water, with a long slim neck and pointed, dagger-like bill. Legs positioned far back provide underwater propulsion but make movement on land awkward; swimming and diving are central to its way of life. Age, sex and similar species Breeding adults carry a double black crest and chestnut-and-black facial ruff. The sexes look alike, and crest size alone is not a reliable way to sex a bird. Most ornaments disappear in winter, leaving white cheeks and fore-neck beneath a dark cap. Chicks have striped heads and necks, with traces persisting in young birds. The long neck, pointed bill and larger build separate it from Little Grebe. Compared with Black-necked Grebe, its bill is longer and straighter and the head pattern differs. Winter identification should combine head shape, bill and body posture rather than rely on colour alone. Habitats, food and behaviour It uses lakes, reservoirs and relatively extensive waters with underwater prey and suitable vegetation for nesting. Outside the breeding season it may move to sheltered coastal water and estuaries. Fish and aquatic invertebrates are captured below the surface, with suitable prey swallowed after capture. Repeated disappearance underwater does not mean that the bird has left the site. Patient observation reveals feeding behaviour without provoking escape. Local abundance depends on water conditions, depth, food and disturbance, not simply the size of a lake. Breeding and life cycle Pair displays include facing one another, head movements and, during some phases, presentation of aquatic vegetation. The nest is built from plant material on the water and usually anchored to surrounding vegetation. A typical clutch contains three or four eggs; both parents incubate and care for the young. Small chicks sometimes ride on a parent’s back, a normal behaviour rather than a sign of injury. They learn to dive and receive food before becoming independent. Water-level fluctuations can undermine nests, so the presence of open water alone does not ensure successful breeding. Distribution and seasonality in the Arab world Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia support local breeding populations supplemented by winter visitors; wintering birds also reach Libya and Egypt. In the Levant it is incorrect to describe all birds as transient. References document limited breeding in Syria, and Lebanon recorded breeding at Aammiq in 2019 alongside winter use of inland waters. The Lebanese checklist places regular winter occurrence mainly from December to early March. November is consequently a useful time to monitor seasonal change, not a guaranteed winter peak. The updated Kuwait list describes a rare passage and winter bird, while the Environment Public Authority directory also records breeding; this does not imply a widespread resident population. North African lake status therefore cannot simply be transferred to the Gulf. Summer presence alone does not prove nesting; a nest, chicks or documented breeding behaviour is needed. Ecological role and conservation The global category is Least Concern, LC, although local populations may be affected. As an aquatic predator it participates in food webs and depends on water quality, accessible prey and stable nesting areas. Pressures include pollution, loss of shoreline vegetation, disturbance, abrupt water-level changes and entanglement in fishing gear. Keep boats and observers away from families, avoid cutting across their route and do not approach floating nests for photographs. Absence from a lake is not by itself evidence of pollution: interpreting the cause requires systematic observation. References AviList 2026 — Podiceps cristatus. BTO — BirdFacts: Great Crested Grebe. articles.title: Great Tit
articles.body: Great Tit Parus major — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and recognition The Great Tit, Parus major, belongs to the family Paridae. Its black head, white cheeks, olive back and yellow underparts crossed by a black central stripe form a distinctive combination. The wings and tail are blue-grey, with a white wing bar. At about 12.5–15 cm long, it is among the larger familiar tits within its range. Identification should use this combination rather than one isolated colour. Age, sex and similar species The male usually has a broader black stripe down the underparts than the female. Posture and feather position can alter its appearance in a photograph. Young birds have yellowish cheeks, a less glossy crown and generally softer markings. Blue Tits are smaller and have a blue crown; Coal Tits lack the conspicuous yellow belly and show a white patch on the nape. These differences prevent confusion between the Great and Coal Tits. A distant image that conceals the belly stripe is not a reliable basis for assigning sex. Habitat, diet and behaviour Woodland, forest edges, orchards and gardens provide habitat, especially where mature trees supply cavities and food. Birds search leaves, twigs and bark crevices, sometimes feeding on the ground. Insects, their larvae and spiders are important foods, with seeds and fruit becoming more important outside breeding. A bird may hold a food item against a perch with its foot while opening it. Mixed-species flocks occur in winter; song and territorial defence become more prominent during breeding. Its varied calls mean that different sounds need not represent different species. Breeding and life cycle Great Tits nest in tree cavities and also use suitable nest boxes. The female builds and incubates, while both parents feed the young. Incubation generally takes approximately 12–15 days, and young remain in the nest for about 16–22 days. These are broad biological ranges, not an identical timetable for every country. Breeding success depends partly on invertebrate availability during chick growth. Observations should avoid opening occupied cavities or disturbing families. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Lebanon’s updated checklist, published in 2020, describes a very common resident breeder, from ravines at roughly 300 m to high-elevation tree habitat; recorded breeding extends from late March to late July. Jordan’s checklist also lists it as resident. In north-western Africa its range extends from Morocco to Tunisia, where biodiversity surveys document wooded habitats. Consequently an October sighting in Levantine or Maghreb woodland does not necessarily mark a new migrant’s arrival: the bird may be resident. Its regional seasonal pattern is closely associated with the distribution of suitable wooded habitats. Ecology and conservation Insect consumption places the species within woodland and garden food webs, while it is itself prey for other animals. Its global conservation category is Least Concern, not a guarantee that every Arab locality is secure. Removal of mature trees, loss of cavities and reduced insect resources can diminish habitat quality. Retaining varied trees and natural vegetation supports feeding and nesting. articles.title: Greater Hoopoe-Lark
articles.body: Greater Hoopoe-Lark Alaemon alaudipes Identity and identification Greater Hoopoe-Lark Alaemon alaudipes belongs to Alaudidae. A long downcurved bill and long legs accompany striking black-and-white wings in flight. Sandy standing plumage conceals that pattern. The hoopoe resemblance concerns the bill, not a crest or membership of the same family. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Open desert plains with sand, gravel and scattered plants provide habitat. It runs quickly for invertebrates and also takes seeds. Song flights expose the wing pattern. Shade and shrubs influence exposure to extreme heat. Breeding and parental care It nests on or close to the ground beside suitable vegetation. Desert field research links nest-site choice with temperature and predation risk. Parents feed the young; rainfall and food influence breeding success, so air temperature alone cannot explain nesting dates. Range and Arab occurrence A widespread desert bird, its range crosses North Africa and Arabia into Asia. Saudi and Kuwaiti sources document residence and breeding. Lebanon, by contrast, has exceptionally rare accidental records rather than routine occurrence. Seasonality and observation Suitable resident areas support year-round birds with local movements. Moderate November hours permit observation from tracks and roadsides without driving across plains towards birds. Bill and wing-pattern records are more useful than sandy body colour alone. Ecological role and conservation Dry-plain degradation, off-road driving and excavation are pressures. Apparently simple desert habitat contains carefully selected feeding and nesting sites. Keeping shrubs and undisturbed ground preserves food, shade and opportunities to breed. References State of Kuwait — Fifth National Report to the Convention on Biological Diversity (2014), bird list. articles.title: Greater Scaup
articles.body: Greater Scaup Aythya marila Identification: a northern diving duck Greater Scaup, Aythya marila, is a compact diving duck of northern latitudes. The adult male combines a dark head and breast, a finely patterned grey back and white flanks. The broad bluish bill, yellow eye and rounded head complete the impression. Unlike a male Tufted Duck, it does not have a long trailing crest. The head may show green iridescence, but reflected colour changes with light and viewing angle and is not a sufficient identification character. Females are brown, usually with conspicuous white around the base of the bill. Some female Tufted Ducks also show pale facial markings, so a white patch alone is not diagnostic. Check the bill, head profile and overall build together. Immature and moulting birds lack the clean adult male pattern and deserve particular care. When a bird flies naturally, the long white wing stripe supplies an additional character. Lesser Scaup is the closest identification problem. Greater Scaup generally has a fuller, more rounded head and broader bill; Lesser Scaup often shows a more peaked rear crown. Posture can change these outlines. A series of views is more useful than one photograph taken while a bird is diving, stretching or compressing its head feathers. Wing pattern and several structural features should support any unusual regional identification. Habitat and food During breeding, Greater Scaup uses northern lakes, pools and wet ground near the boreal forest limit and in tundra landscapes. In winter it often gathers on coastal bays, estuaries and lagoons, although inland lakes can also support important numbers. Its association with salt water is therefore seasonal rather than an absolute requirement. Sheltered and exposed coastal situations both occur within its wider winter range. The bird usually obtains food by diving and swimming below the surface. Molluscs are especially important in winter; insects, crustaceans and plant material also contribute, with diet varying between habitats and seasons. Larger food items may be brought up to be swallowed. A flock can look inactive while many of its members are underwater, so repeated counts help separate genuine changes in abundance from a temporary disappearance beneath the surface. Breeding and development The nest is a shallow, down-lined depression, usually close to water, sometimes on an island or among shoreline vegetation. The female selects and builds it. Neighbouring nests can form loose aggregations, but the species should not be imagined as invariably nesting in a dense colony. Pair formation and courtship precede the northern nesting season; male displays include head and body movements rather than a conspicuous song. BTO gives a typical clutch of 8–11 eggs, female incubation lasting 26–28 days, and fledging at approximately 40–45 days. These are reference ranges, not an exact timetable for every nest. The downy young leave for the water and feed themselves under female supervision. Broods may join together, so a large group of ducklings need not represent the offspring of a single female. The ability to swim soon after hatching should not be confused with independence from safe feeding habitat. Range and seasonal movements Greater Scaup breeds across the northern parts of Eurasia and North America. In Europe, Iceland, northern Scandinavia and Russia are important parts of its breeding geography. Many birds move to lower-latitude coasts for winter. The EURING/CMS atlas shows links from Iceland towards western Europe and from Baltic and Russian areas towards the North Sea. Mediterranean waters hold far smaller numbers than the main northwestern European wintering areas. Males can leave breeding areas for separate moulting sites before the full autumn movement to winter quarters. Available ringing evidence is uneven: many recoveries come from older decades and from hunted birds. It describes real movements but does not prove that every scaup reaching North Africa or Iraq follows the same route. A winter observation establishes a bird's presence at a destination, not its precise breeding origin. Occurrence in Arab countries Morocco's rare-bird committee classifies Greater Scaup as a Palearctic accidental visitor in its 2022 report. This differs from the committee's category for a regular winter visitor. Tunisia's Avibase checklist, maintained by Denis Lepage and hosted by Birds Canada, likewise marks it Rare/Accidental. These are country-level rarity assessments, not evidence of nesting or a predictable annual coastal migration. Iraq has a different documented status: Salim and colleagues' Sandgrouse checklist describes it as a rare winter visitor. That seasonal designation should be retained with its rarity qualification. The available national accounts therefore place Arab observations at the southern margins of this northern duck's range, while distinguishing occasional Maghreb records from rare winter occurrence in Iraq. They do not justify labelling every suitable Arab lagoon a regular wintering site. Conservation and observation BTO reports global Least Concern status, but that should not obscure regional decline. A coordinated European study by Marchowski and colleagues, published in 2020, found a substantial fall in northwestern Europe's wintering population between the late 1980s and 2015–2018, alongside a redistribution towards the north and east. Fishing-net bycatch and deterioration of food resources were important concerns. A rise in one country's counts can coexist with a decline across the wider population. For Arab wetlands, protecting feeding grounds and undisturbed resting water is a useful precaution even where the species is rare. Watch from shore with binoculars or a telescope rather than approaching a flock by boat. Photograph the bill and head from several angles if an unusual record needs documentation, and note the accompanying species. Submit the date, location and identification evidence to the relevant national recording body; an uncertain bird is better left unresolved than assigned a confident but unsupported name. articles.title: Greater Spotted Eagle
articles.body: Greater Spotted Eagle Clanga clanga Identity and identification The Greater Spotted Eagle belongs to Accipitridae and appears in older sources as Aquila clanga. Usually dark and broad-winged, juveniles show conspicuous pale spots on the wing coverts. Separation from Lesser Spotted Eagle requires several features, rather than spotting alone. Habitat and food It uses wetlands and meadows near woodland, hunting small mammals, birds and other prey according to habitat. Its movements connect northern breeding areas with southern wintering grounds, making Arab wetlands part of that journey. Breeding and development Estonia’s Environmental Board conservation plan, approved in 2024, reports usually two eggs and incubation lasting 42–44 days. Young normally become capable of flight at 60–65 days, with parental care continuing after departure before independence. These developmental intervals do not transfer Estonian nesting dates to Arab wintering countries. Arab occurrence and seasonality Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes irregular, scarce passage, while Qatar’s list gives scarce winter presence. Oman’s official 2026 list describes abundant passage and winter visits. These differences highlight the Gulf and Oman in winter without demonstrating local breeding. Observation and conservation The Greater Spotted Eagle is globally classified as Vulnerable (VU) on the IUCN Red List. In parts of its European breeding range, hybridisation with Lesser Spotted Eagle is an additional threat. Observe eagles without disturbing resting sites or publishing sensitive coordinates. Reducing electrocution and poisoning and protecting wetlands are important conservation measures. articles.title: Gull-billed Tern
articles.body: Gull-billed Tern Gelochelidon nilotica Identity and identification Gull-billed Tern Gelochelidon nilotica belongs to Laridae; older references use Sterna nilotica. Its robust body, broad wings and short, thick black bill differ from Sandwich Tern’s longer, finer bill. The complete black cap is absent outside breeding plumage. Habitat and food It takes insects and small prey from land or near the water surface rather than relying on fish-diving. Open land near lagoons, saltpans and estuaries provides suitable habitat. Breeding and development A shallow scrape in sand or mud may contain vegetation. CIESM gives two or three eggs, incubation of 22–23 days and fledging 28–35 days after hatching. These developmental periods do not establish a breeding month in every region. Arab occurrence and seasonality Qatar’s current list describes common winter and passage presence, with records throughout the year; it does not assign resident breeding status. Lebanon’s 2020 checklist instead regards it as a rare migrant after additional records, replacing the older vagrant assessment. In November, Qatar observations fit winter presence, while Lebanon’s list does not describe abundant wintering. Observation and conservation Shallow water and varied open habitats support feeding. Avoid disturbing islands and low ground that may be used by bird colonies. articles.title: House Sparrow
articles.body: House Sparrow Passer domesticus — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and appearance The House Sparrow, Passer domesticus, is a compact member of the Old World sparrow family Passeridae, usually about 15 cm long. Its stout, conical bill is suited to handling seeds. A typical adult male has a grey crown, chestnut at the sides of the head and neck, pale cheeks and a black throat bib. The back is brown and dark-streaked, with a pale wing bar. Females are quieter in pattern, with a buff eyebrow and plain grey-brown underparts. Young birds resemble females; recently fledged birds may retain conspicuous yellow gape edges. Seasonal appearance and similar species The male’s bib looks less extensive in fresh nonbreeding plumage because pale feather tips partly cover the black. Wear exposes more black without requiring the bird to acquire an entirely new throat patch. Eurasian Tree Sparrows have chestnut crowns and distinct black cheek spots. North African identification requires particular care: House and Spanish Sparrows interbreed, producing intermediate birds across a complex contact zone, notably in Algeria. These populations should not all be labelled Italian Sparrow; the recognised Italian Sparrow has a distinct hybrid evolutionary history. Female-looking birds may be especially difficult to assign confidently. Habitat, feeding and social life House Sparrows favour settlements, farms, gardens and the edges of cultivated land. Their close relationship with people helps them occupy otherwise harsh environments, but they are not uniformly distributed through empty desert. Adults eat many seeds and grains, with other foods taken opportunistically. Insects and other invertebrates are particularly important for chicks. A Nubian study found contrasting diets at northern Sudanese and southern Egyptian sites, illustrating local flexibility rather than a fixed menu. Birds forage in flocks, hop on the ground, bathe in water and dust, and communicate through repeated chirping calls. Breeding and life cycle Nests occupy cavities in buildings, other structures or trees; some are more exposed constructions in vegetation. Grass and finer lining material form a sheltered chamber. Pairs may nest near one another, and sites can be reused. British data give typical clutches of 4–5 eggs, incubation around 12–15 days and a nestling period of roughly 15–17 days. Chicks hatch helpless and require feeding. Two or three broods are common where conditions allow. These stages explain why a site needs both nest spaces and nearby feeding habitat, not merely a supply of adult seed food. World and Arab-region distribution Native across much of Europe, Asia and parts of North Africa, the species has been introduced widely elsewhere. Across many Arab towns it is a year-round resident rather than a regular spring-and-autumn migrant. Saudi references describe widespread resident breeding, and Kuwait reports abundant residents around buildings and farms. Lebanon’s checklist likewise identifies a widespread breeding resident. Egyptian studies document resident birds and seasonal changes in local counts; these fluctuations are not proof of long-distance migration. In the Maghreb, hybridisation complicates the map. Breeding dates depend on local conditions, so a single European nesting calendar should not be imposed on all Arab populations. Ecology, pressures and conservation Sparrows consume seeds and invertebrates, feed predators and compete for nest spaces. Their ecological role differs between native and introduced ranges. Global IUCN status is Least Concern, but familiarity does not imply universal stability: long-term declines are documented in Britain. Loss of nesting opportunities and food-rich vegetation can reduce habitat quality, while cats are a locally noted threat in Kuwait. Conserving nesting spaces alongside insect-rich vegetation and seed-bearing plants addresses different stages of the life cycle. articles.title: How Can Farmers Protect Migratory Birds This Autumn?
articles.body: In these very weeks, flocks of white storks (Ciconia ciconia) and herons cross the skies of the Bekaa on their way south, while the olive harvest peaks in the mountains and along the coast — from Lebanon to Syria and Jordan. The two events are not as separate as they may seem. The agricultural calendar that governs our harvest season overlaps in time with the biological calendar followed by millions of migratory birds along the eastern Mediterranean flyway. Our olive harvest: an existing strength worth keeping Unlike some southern European countries where olive growing has shifted to intensive systems with large suction and shaking machines that work at night under floodlights — a practice official bodies there have documented as killing millions of migratory birds sleeping in the trees each year, prompting bans in some regions — harvesting in Lebanon, Syria, and Jordan remains largely manual or done with a handheld comb/shaker, and usually by day within family or community labour. That in itself is a real environmental strength our farmers deserve credit for, not only warnings drawn from others’ mistakes. Keeping this pattern — daytime picking, without turning to suction machines or strong night lighting if operations expand later — is enough to spare Lebanon the fate that hit intensive European olive estates. One practical detail still deserves attention: nets spread under the trees to gather fallen fruit, if left stretched on the ground all night without being lifted or checked in the morning, can hinder birds that feed on the ground near trunks or use neighbouring grassy patches to rest. Lifting or folding the nets at the end of each workday, instead of leaving them out between picking sessions, is a simple step that costs almost no extra time. Grain fields: a refuelling stop that needs no complex intervention Unlike the spring breeding season, when birds focus on the nest and longer-term food, their autumn needs are simpler and more urgent: quick energy, water, and a safe place to rest before continuing. Wheat and barley fields harvested in summer provide that service for free if the farmer leaves them without immediate ploughing for a few weeks, so flocks can use spilled grain as fuel for mountain bottlenecks. A small, low-edged water pond in a corner of the land is also enough to draw noticeable numbers of birds exhausted by the journey. Timing rodenticide in orchards In olive and fruit orchards, some farmers use rodent poisons around trunks or storage sheds. The problem is that raptors such as the common kestrel (Falco tinnunculus) and owls, which feed specifically on these rodents and form a free natural defence line against them, suffer secondary poisoning when they eat a poisoned rodent. Better to avoid these pesticides or cut them back during the peak of passage itself, and rely on resident and passing raptors as the alternative control tool. Living hedgerows: shelter that costs nothing Native shrubs along field edges, instead of wire or metal fencing, give passing flocks safe rest points from wind and predators, plus wild fruit that adds another energy source at this exact time of year. The greatest danger remains the gun, not the plough However careful farming practices become, the first danger to these flocks has nothing to do with agriculture at all: indiscriminate shooting by irresponsible individuals at entire flocks in passage — a practice specialist organisations document every year, and one that sometimes turns into mass slaughter of fully protected species, unrelated to any legally permitted quarry. That is precisely the focus of the current autumn campaign run by the APU unit of MECSHAP in cooperation with CABS, which we recently announced in Sayd to protect migration corridors this season. Alongside that direct threat sits a different kind of environmental harm: military operations in southern Lebanon in recent years left wide destruction of forests and farmland — Lebanese official estimates speak of some 16,000 hectares burned, including thousands of dunams of age-old olive trees, and more than a fifth of the south’s agricultural and woodland area — and the south itself sits on one of the most important flyways millions of birds use between Europe and Africa twice a year. Losing plant cover and natural stopover points there deepens the fragility of flocks already worn down by thousands of kilometres of flight. A shared duty: the farmer’s field and the sustainable hunter’s gun The farmer who waits a few weeks before ploughing, and the sustainable hunter who tells lawful quarry from a protected passing flock, serve the same goal from two places: a living environment able to renew itself season after season. Neither has to sacrifice their interest for the other — only some awareness of when and how farm work is done, so that autumn shifts from a season of risk for birds into a safe passage worthy of Lebanon and the Levant’s long history as a natural corridor for their migration.

articles.title: Hunting Tourism in the Maghreb
articles.body: A hunter at El Koudia in Morocco, as identified by the organiser. From European travel agencies to lodges, guides and local teams: how do hunting trips generate services and income in Morocco and Tunisia, and what does Algeria need to broaden its appeal as a hunting-tourism destination? A trip may begin in an office in Paris or London, but that office cannot deliver a day’s hunting on its own. Behind it are a driver welcoming the group, a lodge preparing rooms, a guide who knows the terrain and a team handling meals and work in the field. Across the Maghreb, these services come together in packages marketed by European and local agencies to enthusiasts who visit for a few days and spend on much more than game. After exploring the Gulf, Sayd turns in this second instalment to a different market: proximity to Europe, programmes for partridge, small game and wild boar, and businesses providing local organisation. Morocco and Tunisia offer commercial examples and statistics that reveal the outlines of this activity, while Algeria raises the question of how hunting regulation can translate into a complete tourism product. A hunting dog carrying game, from DHD-Laïka’s small-game programme in Morocco. Morocco: from three days in the field to a stay in Marrakech According to figures from Morocco’s National Agency for Water and Forests reported by 2M, hunting tourism welcomed around 5,000 visiting hunters during the 2025–2026 season, and the sector comprises 146 specialist companies. This is a base of visitors and organisers extending beyond isolated individual trips. The offers show how European demand reaches Moroccan terrain. French agency DHD-Laïka advertises a programme between Rabat and Tangier with three hunting days and four nights, starting at €2,750 per hunter for groups of five or more. It includes flights from Paris, excluding airport taxes, accommodation, meals, transfers, guides, porters and permits. The package spans international travel and services at the destination; its entire price does not flow into the local economy. In a different model aimed at private groups, Britain’s William Powell Sporting markets El Koudia in the Jbilet hills near Marrakech: two days for eight hunters at an advertised team price of €40,400. Field staff, hospitality, transfers, permits and the equipment specified in the offer are included; hotel accommodation is not. Marrakech also offers non-hunting companions places to stay, sights to visit and shopping, extending the trip beyond time spent hunting. Yet the two products are not the same experience. At El Koudia, the marketer explains that reared birds are released before the season. This differs from a programme based on wild game. Each model requires management and environmental monitoring; neither bird density nor a high price establishes sustainability. The Moroccan organiser also has a place in the legal framework. Hunting-tourism rules link the reception of non-resident visiting hunters to an authorised organiser and require staffing, an investment project and a leased hunting area. The local partner is therefore more than a sales intermediary: it carries responsibilities for managing both the trip and the area. Two hunters in the field during a Tunisian wild-boar drive, as described by DHD-Laïka. more than the price of game Rooms and meals, transport and guiding, field work and fees: these are the services within a hunting trip. Local communities’ share depends on wages, purchases and local contracts, not the package price alone. Hunters and a camera crew after a hunt, with two wild boars; from Chasse Sanglier Tunisie. Tunisia: a clear French market—and teams from villages In Tunisia, the figures provide a tangible picture of visitors and public revenue. The National Report on the State of the Environment and Sustainable Development for 2022 records 606 visiting hunters in the 2021–2022 season, including 532 French nationals. Treasury receipts from hunting tourism reached 300,233 Tunisian dinars. This is a historical total of fees and public revenue associated with the activity, not visitors’ total spending or organisers’ profits. France remains visible in the marketing. DHD-Laïka advertises a wild-boar programme with five hunting days and six nights for €2,390 per person in groups of ten to twelve. It describes employing a team of fifteen to twenty beaters from villages, alongside hotels, transport and local organisation. These services create opportunities for seasonal work in villages, tied to trip dates rather than necessarily providing permanent, year-round jobs. Within Tunisia, Desert Rose offers programmes in Spanish, providing another channel to European customers. The advantage is not simply language: a local agency brings knowledge of the region together with accommodation, transport and group reception. Tunisian regulations give this role practical substance. Hunting tourism is organised by Tunisian travel agencies and hotel establishments under rules that include accompaniment by a guide, insurance and obtaining hunting permits in advance. When a responsible organiser oversees the trip, monitoring participants and game becomes part of the service rather than something left to the visitor. Treasury revenue, not turnover 300,233 Tunisian dinars: Treasury receipts from hunting tourism in the 2021–2022 season, according to the national environment report. The figure does not automatically include spending on hotels, transport and meals, nor establish that all of it was earmarked for nature conservation. Algeria: regulation alone does not create a destination Algerian legislation explicitly addresses hunting tourism, linking it to a tourism agency and specific conditions, including areas where game is artificially bred. The Directorate-General of Forests announced the opening of the 2026–2027 hunting season for 10 October, as reported by Algeria Press Service. Opening the general season, however, is different from making a fully compliant programme available to foreign hunting tourists. Developing this activity into a broader tourism product requires bringing together the elements of the trip: an agency to receive visitors, a suitable hunting area, accommodation, transport, guiding and a clearly defined programme that can be marketed and booked. The Moroccan and Tunisian examples show that geography alone is not enough. What visitors buy is an organised trip from arrival to departure. Mauritania: an opportunity raised in development plans In Mauritania, the operational assessment of the tourism strategy, prepared in 2017 with support from the United Nations Development Programme and published by the ministry, considered the potential revival of hunting tourism under strict, enforced regulation and coordination between the tourism and environment sectors. This approach puts management before expansion. It is a historical planning proposal, not an announcement of a hunting programme operating today. From seasonal income to a lasting resource The Maghreb’s examples show where value can arise: in lodges and hotels, through drivers, guides, cooks and field workers, and in fees collected by the state. Companions and other tourism activities can broaden spending rather than confining a visit to a single day’s hunting. Turning an opportunity into development, however, takes more than increasing visitor numbers. Contracts, wages and local purchasing determine what remains in the area, while training, safety and predictable seasons influence the quality and continuity of work. Game and habitats, meanwhile, require scientific monitoring, quotas and enforcement: pressure on the natural resource can undermine the very activity on which livelihoods depend. Calling a trip “sustainable” in an advertisement is therefore not enough. The test is whether it combines legal, accountable activity with services that benefit local people and management that safeguards the resource for future seasons. At that intersection, hunting tourism becomes more than a brief visit: an opportunity for a local economy that deserves careful organisation, measurement and protection. The prices cited come from commercial offers checked on 23 October 2026, not market averages or confirmation of booking availability. From the series: Hunting Tourism in the Arab Gulf Countries. articles.title: Isabelline Wheatear
articles.body: Isabelline Wheatear Oenanthe isabellina Identity and identification Isabelline Wheatear Oenanthe isabellina belongs to Muscicapidae. Pale sandy plumage accompanies an upright stance and relatively long legs. A dark wing patch and black-and-white tail are useful. Unlike Desert Wheatear, the tail is not predominantly black; head shape, eyebrow and voice help with other wheatears. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour It uses steppe, dry open ground and sparsely vegetated pasture. Running and pausing on the ground, it collects insects and small invertebrates. Stones and soil clods provide lookouts. Dependence on ground invertebrates links it to habitat quality even in apparently sparse terrain. Breeding and parental care A suitable burrow or ground cavity holds the nest, sometimes using small-mammal burrows. Plant material lines the chamber and adults bring food to young. Care continues after nest departure. A bird near a hole does not prove that it excavated it or occupies it for breeding. Range and Arab occurrence It breeds across steppe from southeastern Europe through western and central Asia and migrates or winters farther south. Lebanon has summer breeding in the northern Beqaa and passage. Winter records occur in parts of the Arab region, but national statuses should not be transferred indiscriminately. Seasonality and observation Lebanon’s checklist places spring passage from mid-February to early May and autumn passage beginning in August. November sightings require country and site context rather than the breeding calendar alone. Tail, wing and bill photographs improve documentation. Ecological role and conservation It consumes invertebrates and is affected by steppe conversion, grazing that removes habitat variety and vehicles over burrow sites. Varied open ground is preferable to uniform levelling. Leave holes unopened: they may shelter birds or other animals. articles.title: Jack Snipe
articles.body: Jack Snipe Lymnocryptes minimus Identity and identification Jack Snipe Lymnocryptes minimus belongs to Scolopacidae. Smaller and shorter-billed than Common Snipe, it has a compact body, conspicuous pale back stripes and a dark crown lacking Common Snipe’s pale central stripe. Camouflage plumage does not permit sex or exact age to be assigned from every photograph. Habitat and food It hides in damp vegetation, eating insects, worms and snails. Repeated body-bobbing accompanies feeding. It may remain still until danger approaches; deliberately flushing it to test this behaviour is inappropriate. Breeding and development It breeds in northern marshlands with a concealed ground nest. BTO gives a typical clutch of four eggs and female incubation of 17–24 days. Downy chicks become mobile early; movement does not establish flight capability. Arab occurrence and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes a rare migrant and scarce winter visitor from mid-October to late April, noting that concealment may suppress sightings. Qatar’s current list also gives scarce winter status. November falls within its winter visitor period; few records do not establish absence. Observation and conservation Waterlogged soils and vegetation provide food and concealment. Quiet photography at a distance is preferable to repeatedly forcing the bird into flight. articles.title: Hunting in Jordan: Understanding Licences, Seasons and Species Protection
articles.body: Agriculture Law Article 56: licences, protected wildlife and prohibited methods, distinct from annual season decisions. Al Khazneh in Petra, Jordan Terrestrial hunting in Jordan is governed by a framework combining licences, species protection and restrictions on where and when hunting may take place. Agriculture Law No. 13 of 2015, as amended, is a central reference. Article 56 addresses wild birds and wild animals. This explainer concerns an established framework; it does not announce new legislation or the opening of a hunting season. The Ministry of Agriculture lists the law and its amendments in its official legislation catalogue. The law empowers the agriculture minister to issue instructions covering licensing, hunting areas, dates and protected species. The Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature (RSCN) states that the wildlife protection committee determines areas, seasons and permitted numbers annually, with announcements published through RSCN. Hunters therefore need to check the relevant species, day, location and quota alongside their licence. Last year's dates cannot establish permission for this year. RSCN hunting regulation. RSCN provides an online hunting-licence application service. The ministry's published 2015 service guide also identifies hunting-firearm documentation and Interior Ministry approval within the licensing process. This illustrates why firearm requirements need separate attention. Because that guide is historical, applicants should confirm current documents and charges with the responsible authority rather than treat it as a 2026 checklist. Historical 2015 agricultural service guide. Article 56 sets restrictions beyond licensing. Hunting is prohibited inside nature and grazing reserves and in specified inhabited areas. It also prohibits vehicles, spotlights and automatic weapons in hunting, alongside poisons, adhesives and certain capture methods. Nests, eggs and young animals receive protection, while hunting birds of prey and predatory wild animals requires ministerial approval. Protected species are classified into three lists according to their degree of protection. Agriculture Law, Article 56. Depending on the offence, consequences include fines, imprisonment and confiscation of wildlife, equipment and weapons. The law also provides for increased fines for repeat offences within the specified period. The practical starting point is a valid licence, followed by verification of the official seasonal announcement, species, location and firearm requirements. This article does not confirm that any season is open on its publication date. It is general legal information, not individual legal advice. articles.title: A Jurassic bird that could not fly broadens the story of avian evolution
articles.body: A peer-reviewed Nature fossil study identifies a striking early terrestrial branch of bird evolution. Min Wang / Chinese Academy of Sciences The early history of birds was not necessarily a straight path towards more powerful flight. A newly described Late Jurassic species from southeastern China provides evidence for a different ecological experiment around 150–148 million years ago. The fossil, Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis, comes from the Zhenghe Fauna of Fujian Province. In research published in Nature on 14 October 2026, scientists describe a mosaic of bird-like and dinosaur-like anatomical features. Most notably, the forelimbs were markedly short relative to the rest of the skeleton. Comparative analyses led the authors to infer that this bird lived on the ground and was flightless. Skull, dental and foot characteristics offer further evidence that the earliest avialans followed several anatomical and ecological pathways rather than one universal trajectory. The finding does not settle when flight first evolved, nor does it show that every early bird was flightless. Whether this particular lineage inherited or subsequently lost flight capabilities is part of the larger evolutionary discussion. The discovery matters because it expands the known diversity of Jurassic birds at a time when fossils remain exceptionally rare. Original research: Xu, Wang et al., Nature, 14 October 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10972-z. Original peer-reviewed research

articles.title: The day the King of Jerusalem died while hunting hares
articles.body: AI-generated illustrative image. In 1142, Fulk, king of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, and his wife, Queen Melisende, were staying in Acre when the queen wished to go on an outing outside the city. The king and his entourage accompanied her, heading to a place outside Acre with gardens and fields watered by several springs. Along the way, boys who were ahead of the procession startled a hare hiding among the furrows. Those present raised their voices, and the king seized his lance and urged his horse to chase the hare. But the horse fell during the rush and threw the king to the ground. According to the historian William of Tyre, the saddle struck King Fulk’s head, causing a severe injury. His companions hurried to him and found him unable to speak and unconscious. The procession was thrown into confusion and the queen grieved, while news of the accident reached the people of Acre. The final return to Acre Fulk was carried into the city while he was still breathing. The account says that he remained unconscious for three days and died on the fourth. His body was then taken to Jerusalem, where he was buried in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Fulk ruled the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem alongside Melisende, who held the hereditary right to the kingdom. After his death, the queen continued to exercise power while their son Baldwin was still young. The sources differ on the date of his death. William of Tyre’s text gives the year as 1142, while a study by the historian Bernard Hamilton favours November 1143, based on the sequence of events in the royal family. References within the source also differ on the exact day of his death. Springs and ploughed furrows William’s description gives the incident a setting that extends beyond the story of the chase. The destination, as described in the French translation, was watered by several springs, and the hare emerged from ground with “ploughed furrows”. These details depict a scene on the outskirts of Acre, where water and ploughed land formed part of the place through which the procession passed. The historian did not name the location, but he preserved a fleeting image of the city’s countryside: a king on horseback, a hare emerging from its hiding place, and a brief chase that changed the course of rule. Sources: William of Tyre, A History of Deeds Done Beyond the Sea, Book XV, Chapter 27, and the French translation, pp. 443–445; and Bernard Hamilton, “The Queens of Jerusalem, 1100–1190”. articles.title: Lanner Falcon
articles.body: Lanner Falcon Falco biarmicus Identity and identification Lanner Falcon Falco biarmicus belongs to Falconidae. Slender and long-tailed, adults often show a rufous crown and nape with a narrower dark moustache than Peregrine. Juveniles are more streaked. Geographic variation means separation from Saker and Peregrine requires proportions, head and tail patterns together. It is placed in the order Falconiformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Open rocky country, semidesert and farmland provide hunting habitat. Birds dominate the diet, supplemented by small mammals, reptiles and insects. It pursues prey in flight or attacks from a perch; pairs may cooperate. Hunting behaviour alone does not settle identification. Breeding and parental care It uses rock ledges or another bird’s old nest rather than building a substantial nest. A typical clutch contains three or four eggs; incubation lasts about 32 days. Young begin flying around 35–47 days after hatching and remain dependent on parents. Breeding calendars differ between North Africa and other regions. Range and Arab occurrence Its African and Middle Eastern range includes resident Arab populations in North Africa. Lebanon’s checklist instead describes scarce passage and winter visits without confirmed breeding. Maghreb resident status should not be transferred across the Levant. Seasonality and observation November sightings may involve eastern winter visitors or resident Maghreb birds. Distant photographs require caution with similar falcons. A sequence showing head, wings and tail helps identification without approaching nests or resting places. Ecological role and conservation Prey depletion, habitat loss, egg and chick collection and illegal trade affect wild populations. Quiet nesting sites and enforcement of protection laws matter. Reliable records should also distinguish genuinely wild birds from individuals escaped from captivity. articles.title: Lesser White-fronted Goose
articles.body: Lesser White-fronted Goose — captive birds Anser erythropus A small goose requiring careful identification Lesser White-fronted Goose Anser erythropus is a compact grey-brown goose with a short pink bill, steep forehead and conspicuous yellow eye-ring. Adults have a white blaze rising above the bill and irregular dark marks across the belly. The sexes are similar in plumage; males average somewhat larger, but this is not a reliable character for sexing a lone bird in the field. The principal confusion is Greater White-fronted Goose. Lesser has a shorter bill and a more compact head and neck, while the adult forehead blaze usually reaches higher. Body size alone is unsafe without a useful comparison, and the eye-ring must be seen clearly rather than inferred from a blurred photograph. Juveniles lack the full adult white forehead and dark belly pattern, making age an important part of identification. A young Lesser should not be rejected merely for lacking adult markings. Tundra breeding habitat and winter feeding grounds Its breeding environments include low-Arctic tundra and forest-tundra, often with dwarf shrubs, lakes, streams and sedge marshes. Some birds nest in hilly or rocky terrain rather than on a uniform flat tundra plain. Nearby wet meadows and low vegetation provide feeding opportunities. The species therefore links terrestrial grazing habitat with water used for refuge and rest. During migration and winter it uses short vegetation in coastal meadows, saltmarshes, steppes and other open ground. Agricultural land has replaced much natural habitat in parts of its non-breeding range. A field used for grazing and a wetland used for roosting can be separate parts of the same essential daily landscape; safeguarding one without the other may leave an important gap. Food, flocking and family life The diet is predominantly plant-based, including grasses, sedges and other terrestrial or aquatic vegetation, with agricultural grains also taken in winter. The short bill allows close cropping of low growth. Feeding habitat is not interchangeable simply because it looks green: plant composition, accessibility and disturbance affect its value. Birds may feed alongside other geese, which can conceal a few Lesser White-fronted Geese within a much larger flock. Pairs maintain strong bonds, and young can remain associated with their parents until the next breeding season. Outside nesting, flocking brings individuals together at feeding and resting sites. These family associations are useful to observers but should not encourage approaching closely; repeated displacement costs feeding time and can separate birds from suitable cover or refuge. Breeding and the flightless period Nesting is generally by separate pairs, with a ground nest near water, sometimes sheltered by low shrubs or rocky terrain. It is not characteristically a colonial breeder nesting around raptors. The female incubates while the male remains nearby. The British Waterfowl Association gives a usual clutch of 4–6 eggs and incubation of 25–28 days; other reference works give wider clutch ranges. These figures describe normal variation rather than a fixed output for every pair. The downy young leave the nest before they can fly and must grow while moving between feeding and resting areas. Adults also have a flightless wing-moult period. Quiet refuges with accessible food consequently matter beyond the days of egg incubation. Seeing birds in a northern wetland during summer does not by itself show that they are successful breeders: non-breeders can make separate moulting movements. Several migration systems The breeding range runs discontinuously from northern Fennoscandia across Russia into eastern Siberia. Eastern birds largely winter in China, while western populations use routes towards south-eastern Europe, the Caspian region and the Middle East. Kazakhstan provides important staging areas for western birds. The small Fennoscandian population is a distinct conservation focus within this wider picture, and its movements should not be used as a template for every individual of the species. Tracking and field surveys have clarified routes, but gaps remain, particularly across parts of the wintering range. Reintroduced Swedish birds wintering in the Netherlands also need to be distinguished from naturally established migration systems. Such distinctions matter when interpreting observations: the same species name does not mean that every flock has the same origin, route or conservation history. Arab-country occurrence: wintering and vagrancy Iraq is a documented wintering country in the OSME regional synthesis and international species accounts. It forms part of the western population's non-breeding range, not its Arctic nesting range. The available evidence does not justify extending this wintering status to every neighbouring Arab country or assuming that all Iraqi wetlands hold the species regularly. Oman's official list classifies Lesser White-fronted Goose as a vagrant; OSME records a bird at Khawr al Mughsayl in January–March 2023. For Jordan, OSME cites the first record at Aqaba in February 2017. It also notes occurrence in the United Arab Emirates without establishing regular seasonality. Egypt's EORC 2019 checklist accepts wild occurrence in Category A, but that category is not a wintering-frequency classification. These are different kinds of evidence and should remain separate in any regional account. Threats, documentation and responsible observation The global category reported by BTO is Vulnerable. Unsustainable killing, loss or alteration of feeding and roosting habitat, and disturbance affect populations across their migration routes. Resemblance to the more numerous Greater White-fronted Goose makes identification relevant to conservation as well as birdwatching. Protection has to follow the birds between breeding grounds, staging sites and winter refuges. BTO also notes escapes from waterfowl collections, so an unusual record requires consideration of origin as well as identification. Record rings if visible without disturbing the bird, companions, behaviour, date and locality; neither tameness nor the absence of a ring proves origin. The photograph accompanying this account shows a captive bird and illustrates appearance, not wild occurrence at an Arab locality. articles.title: Libya: three-year hunting ban for wild animals and birds in Sirte
articles.body: The decision covers the city and surrounding areas, including coastal and inland areas and reserves The Libyan Authority for Heritage and Wildlife has banned the hunting of all wild animal and bird species in Sirte and surrounding areas for three years under Decision No. 24 of 2026, according to a report published by the Al-Anbaa al-Libiya newspaper on 5 November 2026. The ban covers coastal and inland areas and reserves within that geographical scope. Its three-year term runs from the date the decision was issued. The relevant authorities have been tasked with enforcing the measure and taking legal action against offenders under applicable legislation. The measure aims to protect wild species and their habitats, reduce the pressures they face and conserve biodiversity. articles.title: Little Grebe: diving among reeds, where residents meet winter visitors
articles.body: Little Grebe A Little Grebe disappears below the surface and reappears away from the observer’s original view. Its small size conceals a busy life: diving for food, building among aquatic plants and sometimes carrying chicks on its back. An autumn sighting is not necessarily a migrant; in several Arab wetlands, residents meet winter visitors. [11] Identity Arabic name: الغطاس الصغير, documented in The Birds of Saudi Arabia. The scientific name is Tachybaptus ruficollis; the French name is Grèbe castagneux. It belongs to Podicipedidae, order Podicipediformes, not the duck family. AviList v2026 includes tricolor within the species while identifying a need for wider review of species limits in this complex. The listed global conservation category is Least Concern, LC. [1] [2] [8] Plumage, age and sex Breeding plumage combines a dark head with chestnut cheeks and foreneck and a pale patch at the bill base. Outside this plumage the face and neck become paler and less contrasting. Young birds retain pale and dark head and neck striping; chick markings should not be mistaken for another species. [6] The sexes look similar, and colour intensity alone cannot reliably sex a bird in an ordinary photograph. The ringing guide gives a length of about 25–29 cm and notes that ageing may require flight-feather examination. Field recognition therefore combines small size, head and bill shape and neck pattern rather than one colour. Several unobtrusive views are more useful than chasing the bird for a closer photograph. [7] Black-necked Grebe Podiceps nigricollis differs in breeding plumage through its black head and neck and golden feather tufts behind the eyes; these seasonal features must not be projected onto a pale winter bird. [14] Arab seasonality: residents and visitors In Saudi Arabia the reference describes a rare breeding resident and common winter visitor, distributed patchily, with winter occurrence from September to March. The UAE’s February 2026 checklist calls it a common resident and locally common migrant and winter visitor; the first confirmed breeding was at Kalba in April 1989. Neither statement means that all Gulf birds migrate or that abundance is uniform across countries. [2] [4] Lebanon has local resident and summer-breeding populations, including at Aammiq, Anjar and Oyun el Samak. The 2020 checklist records winter reinforcement chiefly in November–late February and passage in September–late November and mid-March–late April. The Tunisian study published in 2024 describes it as sedentary and records it during winter 2020–2021. An autumn increase therefore cannot automatically be assigned to arrival from abroad without tracking evidence. [3] [5] An original nesting study confirms breeding at Lake Tonga in northeast Algeria. The IUCN country list also includes Morocco, Egypt, Iraq, Oman, Yemen and Sudan; country inclusion establishes occurrence, not the residency or breeding calendar of every population. Its distribution extends beyond these examples, but local seasonality requires local evidence. [9] [10] In Egypt, the Lake Burullus KBA account lists Little Grebe among breeders, based on historical documentation and a latest assessment dated 2016, not a new count. Iraq’s Central Marsh surveys in October 2013–June 2014 classified it as resident and confirmed breeding through juvenile sightings. [12] [13] Habitat, food and behaviour It uses ponds, lakes, reservoirs and basins combining open water with emergent vegetation, sometimes entering brackish water. Food is mainly insects and larvae, supplemented by molluscs, crustaceans, amphibians and small fish, many caught by diving. An artificial pond can have ecological value, but the presence of a grebe alone does not prove clean water or a healthy ecosystem. [2] Its repeated, whinnying trill may be heard before the bird is seen among plants. Quiet waiting helps connect a call with its source; a sound recording still requires reliable comparison and does not establish a breeding pair or nest. A feeding bird should be distinguished from direct breeding evidence such as an occupied nest or dependent chicks. [11] Nesting and life cycle Both adults build with aquatic vegetation; the nest may float, anchored to plants. They share incubation and care, cover eggs when leaving and may carry chicks on their backs. Early swimming ability is not independence from parental care. [2] [6] BTO reports a typical clutch of 4–6 eggs, incubation of about 20–21 days and fledging at about 44–48 days. These are reference values, not fixed limits for every Arab population. A study published in Ardeola in 2015 followed nesting at Lake Tonga during 2010–2012, with egg laying from late March to late July. This is valuable local evidence, not a calendar for the Gulf or Nile Valley. [8] [9] Ecological importance and threats Its food web includes insects, other invertebrates and small fish, while marginal vegetation and suitable water conditions support nesting. At Lake Tonga, nest success varied with site conditions; predation and flooding were among recorded causes of failure. Site management needs this context before attributing change to a single cause. [2] [9] Least Concern does not mean that every local population is safe. Repeated surveys at the same sites are more informative than comparing two photographs or counts made with different effort. Responsible observers avoid cutting paths through reeds or approaching nests for photographs, record date, place and approximate age where possible, and leave sex undetermined when diagnostic evidence is absent.
