articles.title: Little Owl
articles.body: Little Owl Athene noctua — A small resident owl in diverse Arab habitats, active at night and dusk and sometimes visible by day Identity and recognition The Little Owl, Athene noctua, belongs to the family Strigidae and is also called sada in Saudi references. A compact body, short tail and broad, flat-looking head combine with yellow eyes and pale eyebrows to give it a stern expression. Brown to grey-brown plumage is spotted with white above and streaked below. Birds may sit openly by day on rocks, trees or buildings, bobbing their heads when alert. The species inhabits diverse environments across North Africa, the Levant, Arabia and much of Eurasia. Age, sex and similar species Males and females share similar plumage; females tend to be slightly larger, with considerable overlap in measurements. Young birds have softer, shorter and relatively paler feathers, and facial appearance and markings develop with growth and moult. The broad head without prominent ear tufts, spotted upperparts and undulating flight help distinguish it from small Otus owls with a different outline. Plumage shades vary among regions and subspecies, with many dry-country birds relatively pale. Subspecific identification requires locality and detailed characters, since colour alone can mislead. Habitat, food and behaviour Semi-open country, farmland, orchards, rocky ground and semi-desert provide habitat, together with cavities and lookout perches. Activity is especially marked around dusk and at night, although birds may also hunt in daylight. Prey includes beetles and other invertebrates, small mammals, reptiles and birds, taken from a perch or during a short ground pursuit. Its small size accompanies considerable dietary flexibility. Low vegetation facilitates access to prey, while old trees, walls and rock crevices provide hiding and nesting places close to feeding areas. Breeding and life cycle Eggs are laid in a cavity such as a rock crevice, tree hole or building, and sites may be reused. The Saudi reference describes a typical single brood of three to five eggs, approximately 28–33 days of incubation and about 30–35 days in the nest. The female incubates and tends small chicks while the male brings food; both parents’ participation in care expands as the young grow. These are reference values that vary among populations and conditions. Pairs may remain in their territory year-round, while young disperse in search of places to settle. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist records a breeding resident in many mountain areas and the Beqaa; Jordan’s list also records residence. In Saudi Arabia it is a widespread but uncommon breeding resident, using low rocky areas and cultivated land. AviList 2026 illustrates substantial regional differentiation: glaux occurs in North Africa; saharae in parts of the Maghreb, western Egypt and Arabia; lilith in the inland Levant south to southern Sinai; and bactriana reaches Iraq. Other subspecies occur on Sudan’s coast and in Somalia. Late October forms part of resident occurrence in these habitats; visibility may change with activity and local dispersal of young rather than the arrival of distant migrants. Ecology and conservation Little Owls consume rodents and invertebrates within natural and agricultural food webs, requiring both prey and safe cavities. AviList 2026 lists global Least Concern, while some European populations have documented declines associated with changing habitats and resources. Retaining hollow trees, rocky nesting sites and prey-rich margins helps support them. Quiet observation from a suitable distance allows people to enjoy the birds while leaving resting sites and nests undisturbed. articles.title: Mallard
articles.body: Mallard Anas platyrhynchos — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and recognition The Mallard, Anas platyrhynchos, is a dabbling duck in the family Anatidae. A typical wild bird is about 50–65 cm long. The breeding-plumaged male combines a glossy green head, narrow white neck ring, chestnut breast and grey body; the central black tail feathers curl upwards. The female is mottled brown, with an orange-brown bill carrying darker markings. Both show a blue-violet wing panel bordered with white. Young birds resemble females. During eclipse, adult males also become brownish, so a green head is not a year-round identification requirement. Distinguishing similar birds Compare the wing panel, bill, body proportions and voice rather than relying on brown plumage alone. Female Gadwalls show a white wing patch rather than the Mallard’s blue-violet panel. A female Mallard gives the familiar loud quack; males have a quieter rasping voice. Domestic descendants and hybrids may be unusually large, white, patchy or otherwise unlike textbook wild birds. Their presence in a park does not, by itself, establish a native breeding population. Habitat, feeding and behaviour Shallow lakes, marshes, slow rivers, reservoirs, lagoons and managed ponds can all support this adaptable species. It feeds by picking, dabbling, dipping its head and tipping forwards, also grazing or gathering seeds on land. Foods include aquatic vegetation, seeds and invertebrates; animal food is particularly important during breeding and growth. Mallards often rest communally and mix with other ducks outside nesting territories. Birds accustomed to people may approach closely, while hunted populations can remain very wary. Breeding and annual cycle Pairs commonly form before the breeding season, but this is not lifelong pair bonding. The female makes a concealed, down-lined nest, usually on the ground near water, although unusual elevated sites occur. Clutch size varies: British nest records give a typical 11–14 eggs. The female incubates for approximately 27–28 days and tends the downy young. Ducklings leave the nest soon after hatching, feed for themselves and usually fly at roughly 50–60 days. Adults replace their flight feathers together and are temporarily flightless; sheltered wetlands are particularly valuable during this vulnerable period. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Resident and migratory populations coexist across the wider range; northern breeding birds commonly move south. Arabian occurrence should not be reduced to one calendar. Eastern Saudi records place passage and winter birds broadly from late August to May, with concentrations mainly September–March. Riyadh records include breeding, but the Saudi national account identifies ornamental introductions as the origin of established feral residents. Kuwait reports passage and winter visitors, occasional summer birds and historical breeding. A summer sighting alone therefore cannot establish either wild origin or nesting. In Lebanon, the 2020 checklist records passage and winter presence from August to early April, with local breeding. Morocco supports resident breeders and winter visitors. Ecology and conservation As a consumer of plants and small animals, and prey for predators, the Mallard participates in wetland food webs. Wetland loss, poor water quality, disturbance and shooting can affect local populations; mixing with domestic stock complicates conservation and monitoring. The 2025 global IUCN assessment lists Least Concern but a decreasing population trend. This does not mean every local population is secure. Retaining quiet, vegetated shores, dependable water and connected wetland habitat supports nesting, moulting and wintering birds. articles.title: Meadow Pipit
articles.body: Meadow Pipit Anthus pratensis — An open-country passage migrant and winter visitor Name and identity The Meadow Pipit belongs to the wagtail and pipit family Motacillidae, order Passeriformes. AviList 2026 recognises Anthus pratensis. Kuwaiti references use the Arabic name Jushnat al-muruj, while the Lebanese guide uses Jushnat al-huqul. The scientific name connects records made under these different names. Pipits can look remarkably similar at a distance: plumage, proportions, voice and habitat work together in identification, rather than the mere presence of a small brown bird in a field. Identification Olive-brown upperparts contrast with pale underparts bearing conspicuous breast streaks that continue down the flanks. The legs are pinkish, the bill fine and the hind claw long and relatively straight. The sexes look alike in the field; separating first-year birds from adults requires close examination of moult limits and wing and tail feathers, not a distant photograph. Tree Pipit has a heavier bill, finer flank streaks and a shorter, more curved hind claw. The unstreaked rump also helps separate Meadow Pipit from first-winter Red-throated Pipit. Pale outer tail feathers show in flight, although several pipits share this feature. Habitat, food and behaviour It uses pastures, meadows, open farmland, wetland margins and grassy saltmarshes. Walking through low vegetation, it picks up insects, larvae, spiders and other small invertebrates, adding seeds especially outside breeding. A mixture of short grass and denser cover provides neighbouring feeding and sheltering places. Small flocks occur in autumn and winter; disturbed birds rise with thin calls. On the breeding grounds, the male climbs into the air and descends slowly in a parachuting song display, often making an otherwise inconspicuous bird easier to locate. Breeding and parental care The grass-built cup nest lies on the ground, usually screened by surrounding vegetation. British BTO records give a typical clutch of four or five eggs, incubated by the female for 13–14 days, with young leaving at roughly 12–14 days after hatching. Both parents provision them and care continues after nest departure, which is not immediate nutritional independence. Two broods may be raised. These reference durations from breeding areas are not evidence of nesting in Lebanon, where the species is principally relevant on passage and in winter. Ground nests and young should be left undisturbed. Distribution and migration in the Arab region Its breeding range extends from northwestern and northern Europe to western Russia, with wintering populations moving south into North Africa and Asia. The 2026 Lebanese guide classifies it as a common winter visitor and passage migrant, recorded from early October to mid-April, particularly on the coast and in the Beqaa. Early November therefore falls within its expected season. Kuwait’s rarities committee instead describes it as a scarce passage migrant and winter visitor. Open country in North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean forms part of its winter range, but arrival dates and abundance vary with country, site and weather; this does not imply residence throughout the Gulf. Ecological role and conservation It participates in grassland food webs as an invertebrate consumer and prey for raptors. Conservation data incorporated in AviList 2026 classify it as Least Concern, although declines are documented in parts of Europe. Pressures include altered grazing management, habitat loss, agricultural intensification and illegal hunting. Retaining varied vegetation, field margins and wetland edges is preferable to creating uniform ground cover. Arab-region observers contribute useful records by documenting dates, locations, numbers and diagnostic photographs of birds using winter habitats. articles.title: Naameh night-hunting operation: offenders arrested, vehicles impounded and weapons and equipment seized
articles.body: Field activity in Naameh as part of cooperation between ISF Investigations and APU–CABS. An ISF Investigations operation with field and intelligence cooperation from APU–CABS, following a documented complaint by sustainable hunters. The Mount Lebanon Investigations detachment of the Internal Security Forces (ISF), working with the joint Lebanese–international operations team (APU–CABS) through field and intelligence cooperation, carried out an operation against illegal night hunting in Naameh. It followed a documented complaint submitted by sustainable hunters in the area to the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU). A scene from the Naameh operation involving the Internal Security Forces’ Investigations unit and the joint APU–CABS team. The operation resulted in the arrest of several offenders, the impounding of vehicles and the seizure of weapons and hunting equipment, including hunting guns, lights, electronic devices used to broadcast bird calls and lure birds, and generators. Hunting guns, lights and a generator among the equipment seized during the Naameh operation. The operation is part of ongoing cooperation between the security forces, the joint APU–CABS operations team and sustainable hunters to combat poaching and protect migratory birds and wildlife. Bird-call playback devices, loudspeakers and ammunition among the seized items. These operations are coordinated with the Gendarmerie Command’s operations room and the ISF Public Relations Division. Part of the night-time operation against illegal hunting in Naameh. Image source: Adonis Elkhateeb, Editor-in-Chief.

articles.title: Osprey
articles.body: Osprey Pandion haliaetus Identity and identification Osprey Pandion haliaetus belongs to Pandionidae. Pale underparts, dark upperparts and a dark eye stripe accompany long wings bent at the wrist. Its lighter build, facial mask and plunging fishing technique distinguish it from sea eagles. It is placed in the order Accipitriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour It specialises in fish along coasts, lakes and rivers. Hovering or circling precedes a plunge with feet extended towards prey. Fish-carrying position and hunting behaviour aid recognition, but a raptor above the sea is not automatically an Osprey. Breeding and parental care A large stick nest stands in a tree, on rock or on a suitable platform. Three eggs are usual. References give incubation around 32–43 days and first flight roughly 48–76 days. Young continue receiving food after fledging; males provide much prey while females incubate and young grow. Range and Arab occurrence Globally widespread, it has resident and migratory populations. Coastal nesting occurs in Arabia, while Lebanon has uncommon spring and autumn passage. Not every Arab coastal sighting therefore belongs to a local breeding colony. Seasonality and observation Lebanese autumn passage extends from September to early November, with spring passage chiefly in late March and April. Early November may catch the last local migrants; resident coastal sites may hold birds year-round. Document visible rings without pursuing the bird. Ecological role and conservation Clean water, fish and safe nest sites are essential. Fishing-line entanglement, pollution, disturbance and collisions are threats. Removing abandoned fishing gear and keeping distance from nests reduce avoidable risks, especially near human activity. articles.title: Pallid Harrier
articles.body: Pallid Harrier Circus macrourus Identity and identification The Pallid Harrier is a slender Accipitridae raptor. Males are pale grey with narrow black wingtips, while brown females and juveniles resemble other harriers more closely. Head, wing and tail features should be assessed together before identifying brown birds. Habitat and food It hunts low over plains and grassland, taking rodents, small birds, reptiles and insects. The importance of different prey varies between breeding and wintering grounds, rather than remaining uniform everywhere. Breeding and development It nests on the ground among grasses in its Eurasian breeding range. The Peregrine Fund reports 3–6 eggs, incubated by the female for about 29–30 days while the male supplies food. Chicks first fly at about 6–7 weeks and remain with their parents for several more weeks before independence. Winter presence does not imply local nesting. Arab occurrence and seasonality Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes uncommon but regular passage and rare winter presence. Qatar’s list and Oman’s 2026 list instead describe common passage and winter visits. November encounter prospects therefore differ between the Levant and Gulf; Lebanese rarity should not be extended to Arabia. Observation and conservation The Pallid Harrier is globally classified as Near Threatened (NT) on the IUCN Red List. Important threats include grassland conversion and degradation through overgrazing and fire. Its grasslands and fields benefit from vegetation retention and reduced poisoning and disturbance. For an uncertain identification, several views from a safe distance are more useful than chasing a bird for a closer photograph. articles.title: Pin-tailed Sandgrouse
articles.body: Pin-tailed Sandgrouse Pterocles alchata Identity and identification Pin-tailed Sandgrouse Pterocles alchata belongs to Pteroclidae. Pointed central tail feathers and a white belly distinguish it from Black-bellied Sandgrouse. Males have stronger breast colours and bands, females more cryptic markings. Identification combines belly, tail and head rather than a single feature. It is placed in the order Pterocliformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour It uses steppe, dry plains and open, sparsely wooded farmland. Small seeds are collected on the ground; birds drink regularly and may gather at water. Long pointed wings produce fast flight. A desert flock travelling in one direction is not necessarily undertaking continental migration. Breeding and parental care A simple ground scrape usually holds three eggs. Field studies confirm alternating male and female incubation. Mobile chicks collect their own food, while the male transports water in specialised feathers and both parents protect them. Rainfall, food and regional conditions influence timing. Range and Arab occurrence Its range includes North Africa and parts of the Middle East, including Iraqi steppe populations, as well as Europe and Asia. Lebanon’s 2020 checklist treats it as very rare. Its Arab importance therefore centres on steppe regions rather than common Lebanese occurrence. Seasonality and observation Residence and movements differ among populations. November observation should use distant views of steppe and water, noting arrival and departure directions. Long tail tips may be hidden in a frontal view; several angles help without pursuing birds. Ecological role and conservation Steppe conversion, agricultural intensification, disturbance and hunting are pressures. Nest studies demonstrate sensitivity to human visits; random searching on foot or by vehicle can threaten eggs. Feeding, drinking and nesting habitats require protection together. articles.title: Qatar shooting worlds: 36 Olympic quota places and free finals coverage
articles.body: Illustrative image A total of 1,041 athletes from 91 countries compete in Lusail for world titles and places at Los Angeles 2028. Competition at the shooting world championships began on Tuesday, 3 November, at the Lusail Shooting Complex in Qatar, with 1,041 athletes from 91 countries. They are competing for world titles and 36 quota places for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games, at the opening stage of Olympic qualification. On 12 November, Kuwait’s Abdulrahman Al-Faihan won men’s trap gold after tying India’s Vivaan Kapoor on 29 hits and winning the shoot-off 3–2. China’s Qi Ying took bronze with 22 hits. Kuwait, India and China secured the Olympic quotas, while Kuwait also won team gold with 356 hits. In women’s trap, Italy’s Jessica Rossi won gold with 27 hits, ahead of Guatemala’s Adriana Ruano Oliva on 26 and neutral athlete Daria Semianova on 19. Quota places went to Italy, Guatemala and the Individual Neutral Athletes (AIN) category. On 11 November, neutral athlete Dmitrii Pimenov won men’s 50m rifle three positions gold with a junior world record of 362.8 points. Slovakia’s Patrik Jany took silver with 357.2 and India’s Niraj Kumar bronze with 346.5. Pimenov, Kumar and Norway’s Jon-Hermann Hegg, fourth with 335.9, secured the three Los Angeles 2028 quota places. Jany could not earn a second quota because he had already secured one in 10m air rifle. Quota places do not guarantee the athletes’ own selection for the Games. On 10 November, South Korea’s Yang Jiin won women’s 25m pistol gold with a world-record 44 hits in the final, according to the International Shooting Sport Federation. Vietnam’s Trinh Thu Vinh took silver with 43 hits and China’s Zhang Yueyue bronze with 34. The National Olympic Committees of South Korea, Vietnam and China received the event’s Los Angeles 2028 quota places, without guaranteeing the athletes’ own selection for the Games. On 9 November, Serbia’s Aleksandra Stojadinovic won women’s 50m rifle three positions gold with 358.4 points, finishing 0.7 ahead of South Korea’s Oh Sehee, who took silver with 357.7. Japan’s Misaki Nobata earned bronze with 348.2. The three medallists also secured Los Angeles 2028 quota places for the National Olympic Committees of Serbia, South Korea and Japan. These quotas do not guarantee the athletes’ own Olympic selection, which remains subject to the applicable qualification and selection rules. On 6 November, Egypt’s Azmy Mehelba won silver in men’s skeet and Kuwait’s Abdulaziz Alsaad took bronze, securing Olympic quota places for Egypt and Kuwait alongside gold-winning Denmark. Mehelba had topped qualification with a perfect 125 hits out of 125, equalling the qualification world record. In the final, he tied Denmark’s Jesper Hansen on 34 hits before Hansen clinched gold 16–15 in the shoot-off. Alsaad finished the final with 29 hits. In women’s skeet, China swept all three medals: Jiang Yiting took gold with 34 hits, Che Yufei silver with 32 and Jiang Chaoyu bronze with 27. The Olympic quota places went to China, Slovakia and Kazakhstan. On 5 November, Egypt placed fifth in women’s 10m air pistol team standings with 1,716 points: Hala Elgohari scored 580, Manal Sami 570 and Afaf Elhodhod 566. Elgohari was tenth in individual qualification with 580 points and 15 inner tens, against 580 and 24 inner tens for the eighth-placed finalist. China’s Jiang Ranxin won women’s air pistol gold with 242.4 points, ahead of compatriot Yao Qianxun on 242.1 and Hungary’s Veronika Major on 222.1. China, Hungary and Iran secured the three Olympic quota places. China’s Hu Kai won men’s air pistol gold with 243.9 points, ahead of India’s Jaypal Malviya on 242.2 and Czechia’s Jindrich Dubovy on 220.9. The Olympic quota places went to China, India and Czechia. Sheng Lihao won men’s 10m air rifle gold ahead of Ma Sihan and Miran Maricic. China, Croatia and Slovakia secured the first quota places for Los Angeles 2028. Korea’s Ban Hyojin won women’s 10m air rifle gold on 3 November with 253.1 points, ahead of China’s Han Jiayu and Wang Zifei. Korea, China and France secured the event’s quota places for Los Angeles 2028. On 4 November, Germany’s Florian Peter took men’s 25m rapid fire pistol gold with 33 hits, ahead of France’s Clement Bessaguet on 32 and Jean Quiquampoix on 26. The three Olympic quota places went to Germany, France and Czechia. China also won gold and silver in the 10m air rifle mixed team event that day. Wang Zifei and Sheng Lihao scored 506.1 points, ahead of Du Yuchen and Zhang Changhong on 504.4, while Korea took bronze. The overall championship programme runs from 1 to 14 November, including arrivals, training and departures, while competition takes place from 3 to 13 November. It brings together three main disciplines: rifle, pistol and shotgun. Fixed targets and flying clays In rifle and pistol events, athletes aim at targets over distances that vary by event. These include 10-metre air rifle and air pistol, as well as 50-metre rifle three positions. Shotgun events include skeet and trap, in which athletes attempt to hit clay targets launched by machines. The two events differ in target trajectories and shooting stations, demanding quick reactions, concentration and accuracy. The programme includes men’s, women’s and mixed-team events. The road to Los Angeles Allocation of the championship’s 36 Olympic quota places was completed on 12 November, with the final six awarded in men’s and women’s trap. The quotas were distributed across 12 individual events, with three in each. Earning a quota does not guarantee the athlete’s own participation at Los Angeles 2028, which remains subject to the applicable eligibility and selection rules. Qatar is represented by 22 male and female athletes across skeet, trap, rifle and pistol. Its skeet competitors include Nasser Al-Attiyah and Rashid Saleh Al-Athba, as the hosts seek medals and Olympic quota places. How can viewers follow the finals? The International Shooting Sport Federation is streaming every final live and free on its official YouTube channel, with schedules and results available on its website. Kapa65 / Pixabay

articles.title: Rock Sparrow
articles.body: Rock Sparrow Petronia petronia Identity and names Rock Sparrow, Petronia petronia, is Moineau soulcie in French and belongs to Passeridae within Passeriformes. At about 14–16 cm long, it looks stocky and strong-billed. It is distinct from Pale Rockfinch Carpospiza brachydactyla and Yellow-throated Sparrow Gymnoris xanthocollis. Similar vernacular names, or yellow appearing on two different species, do not make them interchangeable. Including the scientific name is particularly useful when comparing photographs and regional records. Identification Brown and grey dominate, with streaking above and on the breast and flanks. The head is boldly patterned, including a broad pale eyebrow and paler central crown stripe. Adults possess a small yellow throat patch that may be concealed by feathers or viewing angle; failure to see it does not exclude the species. The sexes resemble each other, while juveniles lack the yellow patch. White tips to tail feathers show in flight and complement, rather than replace, the other identification features. Habitat, food and behaviour Stony slopes, short grass, dry farmland and mountain villages provide suitable surroundings, sometimes including old walls and buildings with cavities. Rocks alone are insufficient: birds also need food, accessible feeding surfaces and safe nesting and resting places. Seeds, grain and some fruit are eaten, with insects increasingly important during chick rearing. Birds frequently forage on the ground and become sociable outside breeding. Repeated calls may reveal a flock whose brown plumage blends into earth and stones. Range and Arab occurrence The range extends from southern Europe and North Africa east into Asia. Distribution accounts list resident occurrence in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, as well as parts of the Levant. Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes a common resident mountain breeder, nesting from early April to early August around 1,300–2,200 m and descending in winter. Iraq’s specialist checklist describes a local resident breeder in northern hills and mountains. None of this implies abundance across desert plains or throughout the Arabian Peninsula. Breeding and development Nests occupy rock crevices, wall holes or tree cavities, sometimes in older buildings. A usual clutch contains approximately 4–7 eggs, incubated by the female. References place incubation broadly within 11–15 days and nest departure around 18–22 days, varying among populations, conditions and definitions. Two broods may occur when the season permits. These ranges are more useful than a universal single-day figure, and never justify opening cavities to check development. Repeated adult visits do not warrant inserting a camera into an entrance. November and responsible observation In November, consider elevation as well as country. Increased numbers at a lower site may represent descent from nearby mountains rather than long-distance migration across borders. Watch slopes and adjoining fields from existing tracks and record approximate elevation, flock size, weather and feeding surfaces. Repeat visits to one site make changes easier to interpret than a lengthy pursuit of a moving flock. Do not flush birds to expose their white tail spots; wait for natural movements between feeding and resting places. Conservation Globally Least Concern, the species still benefits from protection against quarrying, damaged slopes and removal of vegetation or cavities. Suitable mountain landscapes combine open feeding ground with hiding and nesting places; losing either can matter even when the other remains. Repairs to occupied walls or buildings require attention to season and local law. Local abundance is neither permission to shoot birds or damage nests nor evidence that every population is secure. articles.title: Ruff
articles.body: Ruff Calidris pugnax — beyond the spectacular breeding ruff The current name The Ruff is Calidris pugnax, a member of Scolopacidae within Charadriiformes. AviList 2026 places it in Calidris. Philomachus pugnax, still found in older books and databases, is an earlier combination for the same species, not another bird. Its Arabic name, al-naffash al-mushakis, evokes the displaying, competing males; it does not mean that the species habitually attacks other birds. This is a wader whose appearance changes dramatically between the breeding season and autumn. Lebanon’s 2026 guide uses the Arabic name durayja sharisa. Breeding finery is not winter plumage Many breeding males carry an extravagant neck ruff and head tufts, varying from white to black and reddish brown. Males are markedly larger than females, but non-breeding birds lack this conspicuous finery. Look instead for a small head, relatively long neck and a moderately short bill with a slightly drooping tip. Leg colour varies and is unreliable alone. Juveniles often have a warm-toned face and breast and neatly pale-edged upperpart feathers. White patches beside the tail base help in flight: structure and several plumage characters matter more than the famous ruff. Finding it among other waders A small female can be confused with other sandpipers, while a larger male in the same flock may look surprisingly different. Size differences alone do not establish different species. Head and bill proportions and the pattern of white in wings and tail help separate it from Common Redshank; structure and plumage also distinguish Wood Sandpiper. Distant photographs may remain inconclusive. In autumn and winter, seeing a Ruff without a ruff is normal, not evidence that the photograph has been misidentified. Feeding and breeding It uses wet fields, flooded grassland, pools and muddy margins rather than being restricted to the sea. It takes invertebrates from land and shallow water and also eats plant material and seeds. Outside breeding it gathers in flocks, sometimes mixed with other waders. Breeding occurs in northern Eurasian wetlands, where males assemble at display grounds visited by females. The female incubates and cares for the chicks; males do not provide brood care. Nests are on the ground and chicks are mobile after hatching. Many birds winter in Africa, with wintering areas also extending into southern Asia. Seasons in Arab countries Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes common to abundant passage, with autumn movement from early August to mid-November and scarce winter occurrence at some coastal sites. An early-November sighting may therefore represent late passage rather than an established winter flock. Kuwait lists uncommon passage and rare winter occurrence, with summer visits that do not establish breeding. Oman, by contrast, lists abundant passage and winter visitation. Moroccan waterbird counts document winter presence. These local categories should not be transferred across the entire Gulf or Levant: water conditions, season and management of surrounding fields shape a site’s value. Lebanon’s 2026 guide confirms abundant passage and scarce winter occurrence. Conservation and responsible conduct Its global category is Least Concern, but wetland loss, grassland conversion, pollution and disturbance can reduce feeding and breeding habitat. A mosaic of pools and wet fields can matter as much as a large lake. Watch flocks from a distant edge without repeatedly flushing them, especially while they refuel on migration. Conservation status is not a hunting permit, and the species’ exceptional plumage variation warrants caution before identifying a distant bird or photograph. articles.title: Sand Partridge
articles.body: Sand Partridge Ammoperdix heyi Identity and identification Sand Partridge Ammoperdix heyi belongs to Phasianidae. Small and rounded, it has sandy plumage and white-and-chestnut flank bars. Males show a grey head with black-and-white markings; females are plainer. Size and head-and-neck pattern separate it from Barbary Partridge and Chukar. It is placed in the order Galliformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Dry rocky slopes, wadis and sparsely scrubbed hills provide habitat. It runs between rocks and collects seeds, plant material and insects on the ground. Birds may gather near water. Camouflage often makes calls or movement easier to detect than a stationary individual. Breeding and parental care A ground hollow is sheltered by rock or vegetation. The female incubates; downy chicks can walk and collect food while accompanying adults. Mobility is not fully developed flight. Local breeding information remains uneven among countries, so figures from one population should not be imposed throughout the range. Range and Arab occurrence Its dry-country range includes Egypt and Sinai, Jordan and parts of Arabia. UAE national assessment records describe breeding in suitable habitat. Lebanon has an old accidental record, rather than evidence of a widespread local partridge. Seasonality and observation Resident in parts of its range, it makes local movements with water and food. Quiet rocky wadis can support November observation, especially in moderate temperatures. Give family groups room to walk away without repeated forced flights. Ecological role and conservation Populations need intact slopes, shelter and safe resources. Vehicle pursuit, excessive hunting and excavation are pressures. Staying on tracks and avoiding refuges protects a bird adapted to running and concealment in exposed arid terrain. References UAE National Red List — Ammoperdix heyi. articles.title: Sardinian Warbler
articles.body: Sardinian Warbler Curruca melanocephala — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and recognition The Sardinian Warbler, Curruca melanocephala, is a small member of the family Sylviidae. Older literature uses Sylvia melanocephala for the same species. At about 13–14 cm long, it has a relatively long dark tail with white outer tips and a red eye-ring. Its English name does not confine it to Sardinia: its range includes Mediterranean habitats and adjoining Arab regions. Age, sex and similar species An adult male has an extensive black hood surrounding the eye, a white throat, grey back and grey flanks. The female has a greyer head, browner back and pale underparts with buff-toned flanks. Juveniles are less contrasting; absence of a black hood alone does not establish a female. Blackcaps have a cap rather than this extensive hood and lack the characteristic red eye-ring. Cyprus Warblers may show dark throat spotting, while Spectacled Warblers have a chestnut wing panel. Females and young birds require several features to be checked together, not identification from a single head colour. Habitat, diet and behaviour Mediterranean scrub, open woodland with dense undergrowth and orchard edges provide habitat. Birds move within cover and flick their tails; a repeated harsh call may reveal them before a clear view is possible. They collect insects and other small invertebrates from foliage and twigs and also eat fruit. This varied diet allows exploitation of seasonally different resources. Concealment should not be confused with absence. Combining visual and acoustic observations improves detection, while repeated playback can unnecessarily disturb birds occupying a territory. Breeding and life cycle A cup nest is built low inside a shrub, and both members of the pair participate in incubation and caring for young. Clutch size and breeding dates vary geographically. Lebanon’s updated checklist records breeding from late March to late July. Dense shrubs supply nesting and concealment sites, so cutting an occupied bush can destroy the family rather than simply remove cover. Evidence such as an occupied nest or dependent young is needed to confirm breeding: a summer sighting alone is insufficient. Incubation usually lasts 12–15 days. Young generally leave the nest 12–14 days after hatching and receive parental care for another two to three weeks. These are general reference ranges that vary among populations. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes a very common resident breeder, reaching approximately 1,600 m in the north, as well as common passage and winter birds from mid-September to late April. October can therefore bring residents and arrivals together. It is listed as resident in Libya, while its broader range includes parts of North Africa, the Levant and Sinai. The AlUla bird guide records winter occurrence in western Arabia, including Harrat Uwayrid, AlGharameel and Wadi Nakhlah. In Oman, the regional reference documents vagrancy, contrasting with winter occurrence in western Arabia. Ecology and conservation The global IUCN assessment conducted in 2018 classified the species as Least Concern, with an increasing global trend. Invertebrate and fruit consumption places it within scrubland food webs. Removing vegetation or changing its structure can affect suitable sites. Cyprus sources also list it among birds harmed by illegal trapping. Maintaining connected patches of structurally varied scrub, woodland and gardens supports both residents and seasonal visitors. articles.title: Saudi Arabia's Environment Law: Hunting permits and wildlife safeguards
articles.body: A reference guide to the Environment Law, hunting permits, protected wildlife and seasonal implementing decisions. Qasr al-Farid in Hegra, Saudi Arabia A Saudi hunting-season announcement does not, by itself, establish what may be hunted, where or with which equipment. The legislative foundation is the Environment Law, issued by Royal Decree M/165 on 10 July 2020, alongside its terrestrial-wildlife hunting regulations. It replaced the previous Wild Animals and Birds Hunting Law of 1420 AH. Bureau of Experts: Environment Law. The regulations require a hunting licence and empower the National Center for Wildlife to set species, quotas, locations, dates and permitted methods. They protect endangered species, pregnant animals, young, nests, eggs and habitats. Protected areas have specific controls; a seasonal announcement does not automatically open them. Regulations, Articles 3–8. A weapon licence neither replaces a hunting permit nor establishes that the weapon may be used for every quarry species. NCW guidance requires permits through Fitri and compliance with approved species and methods, prohibiting mass-capture equipment and unauthorised attraction or calling methods. Check the applicable permit conditions and decision rather than a circulated image or an earlier season's announcement. NCW regulatory guidance. Article 7(2) prohibits hunting with firearms of any type, except within private hunting enclosures specifically licensed by NCW and subject to its conditions. Regulations, Article 7. The penalty schedule officially published in September 2024 lists first-offence fines of SAR 10,000 for hunting without a licence, and SAR 5,000 for hunting in a prohibited location or period. These examples do not exhaust potential penalties or compensation. Official penalty schedule. NCW's official FAQ also warns that displaying hunted wildlife outside vehicles, on roads or online is an offence. Publishing a souvenir photograph is therefore not outside the regulatory framework. NCW FAQ. This reference explainer was prepared on 15 October 2026. It announces neither new legislation nor a season opening and is not legal advice. Consult updated texts, seasonal decisions and permit conditions before travelling. articles.title: Sayd Returns… And This Is What We Want to Offer You
articles.body: Adonis Al-Khatib Adonis Al-Khatib, editor-in-chief of Sayd. When we founded Sayd, we set out from the conviction that hunting is responsibility, culture, and knowledge of nature and the principles of practice. A person who goes out into nature needs to know its birds and animals, understand its seasons and respect its limits, and grasp the effect of their practice on the life around them. Today, as we work on relaunching the magazine, we carry that conviction into a new stage. We want Sayd to become a trusted Arab reference for sustainable hunting and the world of nature, and a platform that joins scientific knowledge with human experience and responsible practice. What does that mean for the reader? And what will they find in Sayd in the coming stage? They will find, first, knowledge they can return to. We will work to present documented material on birds, wildlife, and biodiversity: How do we distinguish species? What do we know about their behavior and habitats? Why do they migrate, and what dangers do they face? And how do we enjoy watching and photographing them and contribute to protecting them? We want the image to help recognition, the fact to rest on a source, and the article to leave the reader with a deeper understanding of what they see in nature. When knowledge is unsettled, we will state its limits; when a fact needs correction or updating, we will review it. Hobbyists and professionals in these activities will also find a space that addresses their practical questions. Responsible hunting, shooting, equestrianism, falconry, and sea fishing have a place in this magazine, as do travel gear, safety, and good preparation. We will cover these fields with help from people of experience, in a way that joins practical benefit with respect for the law, the environment, and sound practice. Laws and seasons will have a clear presence, with a distinction between enforceable texts and demands and proposals. Our position is to support a clear legal season grounded in knowledge and accompanied by real enforcement and serious monitoring. We reject random and illegal hunting, the targeting of protected species, and practices that deplete wildlife. We want the responsible hunter to be a partner in protecting nature, and for that role to show in their behavior, knowledge, and stance. Our return comes as autumn and the bird migration season approach, with the opportunity they bring for knowledge, watching, and photography, and the responsibility toward birds on passage and their habitats. This season will be among the first gateways of our editorial work, alongside following developments in equestrianism, shooting, and nature issues. People and their stories have a fundamental place in Sayd. From the magazine’s beginnings, in-depth interviews were part of its character. In the coming stage, we want to continue dialogue with influential figures in Lebanon, the Arab world, and beyond: officials, businesspeople, artists, riders, and hunters, and with experts, researchers, photographers, and people of distinctive experience. What matters to us in these encounters is what experience reveals: How did their relationship with nature and this hobby begin? What did they learn? How did their view of nature and responsibility change? And what can they offer others? We aspire to build an Arab archive of testimonies and stories worth preserving and reading again. We will work, gradually, to expand Sayd’s presence at specialized championships, exhibitions, and festivals, from Lebanon to Arab countries—especially the Gulf—and to open space for international experiences that add knowledge and expertise. We also want to introduce readers to serious clubs, associations, initiatives, and projects, and to convey the questions and challenges of those working in these sectors. Although “Hunting and Equestrianism” is our main title, the world we belong to is wider. In ecotourism there is a chance to discover a place and respect it; in heritage, a memory of the human relationship with the land; in photography and art, other ways of seeing nature. “Your Health in Nature” and “The Kings’ Table” also have their place, treated with care for accuracy and linking knowledge to experience and local culture. We return with an archive that encourages this work. Older pieces on hunting, shooting, laws, and birds have kept receiving readers years after publication, even during periods of reduced activity. That stock places on us the responsibility of reviewing and renewing it, preserving its value, and adding what deserves to join it. This vision will not be complete in a single day. We will begin with selected pieces and coverages that can be delivered, and develop our presence and sections gradually, while improving the reading experience and access to content—especially on mobile. We will listen to readers and specialists, because their questions and notes are part of building a useful magazine close to its audience. And we want this return to last. Therefore we welcome cooperation with institutions, associations, and companies that share our respect for nature and value specialized media. Accuracy of information and independence of editorial decision will remain the basis of any sponsorship or partnership; the reader’s trust is what gives this work its worth. This is our invitation to our longtime and new readers, and to everyone who has knowledge, experience, or a story worth telling: share your questions and expertise with us, and help us widen this Arab space for sustainable hunting and the world of nature. Sayd returns to be closer to its readers, deeper in knowledge, and clearer in its responsibility toward nature and people.

articles.title: Shireen Bou Rafoul: From valley to valley, the hunters couldn’t stop her!
articles.body: Shireen Bou Rafoul monitoring hunting violations. She loves hunting and considers it part of her identity. But when the choice is between a hunting trip and a mission to rescue a bird, she chooses anti-poaching work. The director of the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU) tells Sayd about the moments from the field that stay with her: a wing trapped beneath a stone, a stork resting its head on her hand, and a kestrel that regained its sight and its freedom. One of the honey buzzard’s wings was injured; a stone pinned down the other, preventing it from escaping. When Shireen Bou Rafoul found it in the field, it was trying to pull its wing out from beneath the stone to free itself. That struggle stayed with her, becoming one of the scenes she recalls whenever she thinks back to her beginnings in bird protection. Shireen did not come to this work out of opposition to hunting. She was a hunter, and still says: “I really, really love hunting. It’s part of my identity.” But between the hunting she loves and a bird left injured and trapped, she found a line she chose to draw. She began taking part in the activities of the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching (MECSHAP) and felt she belonged there. She volunteered to lead the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU). The work gradually took up more space in her life until it became, in her words, “an inseparable part” of it. From one valley to the next, Shireen travels on anti-poaching missions throughout Lebanon, without exception: from north to south, from the Bekaa to the mountains and the coast. While some hunting offenders complain about Shireen and her work in the field, many hunters committed to sustainable hunting support her, reporting violations or injured birds they find. Between the offenders’ complaints and these hunters’ support, she carries on with her missions, taking with her stories that do not end when the patrol is over. Shireen Bou Rafoul at work in the field. Shireen Bou Rafoul on a field mission to rescue a bird of prey. A stork’s head on her hand There is another encounter she cannot forget. The unit’s veterinarian was operating on a stork’s wing, which Shireen was holding steady. The bird turned its neck and rested its head on her hand. “It couldn’t do anything except rest its head on my hand,” she says, recalling the moment as she experienced it. She remembers the effect of that gesture: an injured bird, a wing in the veterinarian’s hands, and a head coming to rest on her own hand. Since then, the suffering of birds wounded by gunfire has felt closer to her. Protection was no longer an abstract idea; it became bound up with birds she had held and helped treat, and others the team could not save. A kestrel with its eyes sewn shut During a campaign this autumn, Shireen faced another scene of cruelty. According to her account, the team came across someone using a kestrel to lure a peregrine falcon. The kestrel’s eyes had been sewn shut. The kestrel was alive and flapping its wings, deprived of sight so it could be used as bait. Shireen can find no words to soften the brutality of what she saw: “Can you imagine someone sewing your eyes shut while you’re alive?” The team took the bird and removed the thread. As she recounts it, the kestrel needed some time to regain its sight before it was released and took flight again. This time, the story ended in freedom. But fieldwork does not offer those who do it the same ending every time. The kestrel. A peregrine they could not save While on patrol, her colleagues found a peregrine falcon in critical condition. To give it the most carefully informed treatment possible, Shireen says the team contacted a falcon hospital in the United Arab Emirates and sent X-rays. According to her account of the consultation, the fractures were severe, and the possibility of poisoning from lead in its body was also raised. Hope remained, and attempts to save it continued, but it died. “We were all upset,” she says. It was not the first time a bird had arrived with injuries beyond the ability of those trying to save it. Yet the loss did not make them give up. She says it strengthened their determination to protect whatever they could, before an injury became another story without a happy ending. When hunters and bird protectors work together Shireen Bou Rafoul, director of the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU). During hunting seasons especially, Shireen receives calls and complaints at all hours and sets off with her assistants on urgent missions to rescue injured birds or free captive birds of prey. She calls on the security forces for missions that require their presence. Many photographs document her alongside security personnel as they address hunting violations, draw up official reports and confiscate hunting guns. She accompanied them on the latest campaign, which included the removal of more than 38,000 square metres of nets used to kill birds. Shireen Bou Rafoul removing hunting nets in cooperation with the Internal Security Forces. From valley to valley.. with the CABS team Shireen praises the readiness and rapid response of Internal Security Forces personnel, considering their presence crucial to completing the missions. She also describes cooperation with the Committee Against Bird Slaughter (CABS) as one of the foundations of the work’s success. She finds particular significance in an organisation dedicated to combating the killing of birds working alongside a centre rooted in sustainable hunting. Shireen Bou Rafoul on a joint mission to address hunting violations. For her, this is not a confrontation between every hunter and every defender of birds. She sees proof in people who once committed serious violations and now help protect birds, report offences and raise awareness. These changes give her more hope than any general talk about the possibility of change. War and the hardest question The hardest thing she faced this year did not concern a bird alone. During the war, confronted with destroyed homes, families losing their loved ones and children dying, Shireen found herself questioning her ability to carry on with the work. How could she rush out into the field to protect birds while family and friends were suffering and she was unable to stop what was happening to them? She recounts how the team tried to help however it could. After conditions grew relatively calmer, she returned to her mission. This did not mean forgetting people’s suffering, but returning to what she could do: “If everyone does their part, everything falls into place.” Shireen does not sum up the reality of illegal hunting with a single verdict. She sees violations declining in some places and changing form in others, and observes that financial pressures are pushing some practices towards trade. She understands the difficult circumstances, but does not see them as a justification for poaching. Nor does the work end at nightfall. She speaks of patrols and joint missions to combat illegal night hunting, of awareness-raising and of offenders being arrested by the competent authorities. As for a hunting trip she might want to take herself, that remains possible when she is sure no other mission is waiting for her. When the two choices coincide, she does not hesitate: “I definitely prefer and choose anti-poaching work.” From the honey buzzard beneath the stone to the kestrel that could see and fly again, hunting has taken on another dimension in Shireen’s life: knowing when to go into the field, not to return with a bird, but to let it return to the sky. Photos: Anti-Poaching Unit (APU)

articles.title: Slender-billed Gull
articles.body: Slender-billed Gull Chroicocephalus genei Identity and identification Slender-billed Gull Chroicocephalus genei belongs to Laridae; older classifications use Larus genei. A relatively long bill and white head without a dark summer hood are useful features; the breast can appear pinkish. Neck length, head shape and bill should be considered together when separating it from Black-headed Gull. Habitat and food It uses saline lagoons, saltpans and shallow coasts, taking fish and invertebrates. Non-breeding gatherings occur around feeding and resting areas; winter presence does not demonstrate nesting. Breeding and development Colonies nest on low ground or islands near water. The CIESM guide gives two or three eggs, about 25 days of incubation and 4–5 weeks of chick rearing. These reference durations are not a single breeding calendar for every country. Arab occurrence and seasonality Qatar’s current list describes a common winter visitor. Lebanon’s 2020 checklist instead describes an uncommon winter visitor and irregular spring migrant. November is relevant to Qatar’s wintering birds and the approaching cold season in Lebanon without implying equal abundance. Observation and conservation Changes to saltpan water regimes, coastal infilling and colony disturbance affect habitat. Observe at a distance and do not publicise active nest locations. articles.title: Socotra Cormorant
articles.body: Socotra Cormorant Phalacrocorax nigrogularis A regional seabird beyond the island in its name The Socotra Cormorant, Phalacrocorax nigrogularis, is a marine member of the cormorant family, approximately 80 centimetres long. Its core range surrounds the Arabian Gulf, Gulf of Oman and southern Arabian Peninsula. Its name does not mean that it is confined to Socotra Island, nor is it simply a dark-plumaged Great Cormorant. Its breeding sites, seasonal movements and threats deserve attention in their own right. Dense flocks can create an impression of limitless abundance, yet concentrating thousands of birds on relatively few islands makes those islands more important, not less vulnerable. Siniya Island in Umm Al Quwain is a significant breeding site among other regional colonies. Numbers on an individual island may change because birds have moved from a neighbouring site, rather than because the overall population has grown. Recognising adults and young birds Adults are sooty dark, with a slimmer head and neck and a finer bill than Great Cormorant. They lack the same extensive white face and chin patch. Breeding plumage gains a greenish or purplish gloss and may include fine white filoplumes around the head and neck. Both sexes share the dark appearance, so blackness or sheen alone cannot establish sex. Immatures are grey-brown above, with pale feather edges on the wings, and lighter below with brown spotting. They can be confused with immature Great Cormorants, Phalacrocorax carbo, which visit some of the same coasts. Combine the slender head and neck and bill shape with face and breast pattern. A pale belly or a large flock is insufficient to identify the species, and a place name cannot establish a bird’s identity. Group fishing below the surface The species feeds mainly on small fish pursued by diving from the surface. A tracking study of birds breeding at Siniya documented overlapping feeding areas and large gatherings at sea. Its results suggest that aggregation helps birds locate and exploit fish schools. They do not establish that a flock follows one leader or divides tasks in the manner of a human team. A dietary study at Siniya during the 2011–2012 and 2012–2013 breeding seasons found that dominant prey shifted from flying fish and sardines to anchovies. The most frequent prey had limited overlap with the local commercial catch. This is a finding from one place and two seasons, not a rule for every sea and year, but it shows why flock size alone cannot demonstrate damage to fisheries. From colony to egg Socotra Cormorants breed in dense island colonies, using shallow ground scrapes rather than nests suspended in trees. Clutches usually contain two or three eggs. The ground around nests also needs protection: an adult leaving as a visitor approaches may expose eggs to heat or predators even when nobody touches the nest. A study published in 2017 followed breeding at Siniya during 2011–2015. It recorded the start of laying between 13 September and 6 October and estimated incubation at 24–27 days. These dates and durations describe a studied population, not a universal timetable for every island. Variation within a colony also means that nests can be at different stages during the same visit. Chicks and gatherings after hatching Chicks begin life dependent on their parents for food, then grow and leave the immediate nest site to join gatherings of young birds. This transition does not mean that every chick can fly or feed independently. An apparently mobile group can contain birds at different stages of parental dependence, so protection does not become unnecessary once eggs are no longer visible. Research at Siniya shows that hatching success and chick survival are affected by colony conditions. Predation studies also demonstrate that terrestrial predators can place additional pressure on birds and eggs. Addressing that pressure requires site-specific scientific assessment, not improvised intervention by visitors. Protecting the breeding cycle involves nesting ground, routes towards the sea and the waters from which parents bring food. Arab range and the November scene The Arab range includes the coasts of Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Yemen; the Convention on Migratory Species also lists Kuwait and Somalia. Country presence does not imply breeding or equal abundance in every country. The Qatar Bird Observation Group describes it as a resident breeder, whereas the Kuwaiti checklist distinguishes occurrence from breeding and lists it as a non-breeder there. In the northern Emirates, autumn is associated with conspicuous breeding activity. A scientific review describes a season generally extending from August to December, sometimes longer after delays or disruption. The studies it assembles indicate that some Siniya birds begin moving towards Abu Dhabi waters in December. November may therefore involve chick provisioning and colony activity rather than merely passage migration, with the situation differing among sites. Vulnerable despite impressive flocks The global Red List category is Vulnerable, VU, also confirmed by the Convention on Migratory Species and BirdLife. Threats include development of coasts and islands, disturbance at breeding sites, marine pollution and entanglement in fishing gear. Losing one colony matters when breeding is concentrated in a limited set of places; a large flock elsewhere does not necessarily compensate for that loss. The best observations leave birds where they are: use binoculars at a suitable distance, avoid landing in colonies and never drive a boat through feeding flocks. Do not collect eggs or chicks or feed birds to attract them to a camera. Repeated, coordinated counts across sites help explain movements. One photograph cannot establish either recovery or decline throughout the region. articles.title: Spanish Sparrow
articles.body: Spanish Sparrow Passer hispaniolensis Identity and names Spanish Sparrow, Passer hispaniolensis, is Moineau espagnol in French; Arabic usage includes both “Spanish” and “Andalusian” sparrow. It belongs to Passeridae within Passeriformes, measures approximately 15–16 cm and has a wingspan of 23–26 cm. Its name does not restrict it to Spain: Mediterranean and Asian populations include both residents and migrants. Separating it from House Sparrow requires more than judging size or noting proximity to people. Identification Adult males have chestnut crowns and napes, white cheeks and extensive black on the throat and breast, continuing as bold flank streaks. The strongly patterned back and substantial bill add useful clues. Winter males look less sharply marked. Females and juveniles are much harder to distinguish from House Sparrows; a pale eyebrow or one mark cannot settle every identification. Hybridisation in North Africa adds further difficulty, making “unidentified sparrow” preferable to forcing an uncertain bird into a species. Habitat, food and behaviour Farmland, fields, shrubs and scattered trees are important habitats, including sites close to water. Seeds and grain dominate the diet, with invertebrates especially important to growing chicks. It is sociable when feeding, roosting and breeding, sometimes gathering in large numbers. A count over a field alone does not measure crop damage: the crop, its growth stage and the birds’ behaviour must also be considered, distinguishing birds collecting fallen grain from those feeding directly on a standing crop. Range and Arab occurrence Its range includes North Africa, the Levant and parts of Central Asia. Morocco recognises it among agricultural birds, while Algerian studies document breeding and hybridisation with House Sparrow. Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes an uncommon summer breeder, common passage migrant and scarce winter visitor. Kuwait supports resident breeders and winter visitors, with colonies recorded at farms and reserves. Oman’s published list describes uncommon passage and winter occurrence. A single seasonal label therefore cannot represent all these countries. Breeding and development Breeding often occurs in colonies. Bulky nests made from grass and other plant material occupy trees or bushes, sometimes beside larger birds’ nests. Clutches commonly contain several eggs, with approximately 3–6 reported and local variation. Incubation lasts roughly 11–14 days and young leave after about 12–15 days. Both parents contribute care, and more than one brood may follow when conditions allow. These intervals are not fixed local dates, and a communal roost is not necessarily a nesting colony. November and responsible observation November offers opportunities to compare field flocks and changing numbers, particularly where winter visitors join residents. One Lebanese flock does not make the species a nationally common winter bird. Record approximate numbers and identifiable males, photographing cheeks and flanks from a fixed distance. Do not use weak streaking on a small or distant bird to prove it is a female House Sparrow. Light and feather edges may obscure markings that appear clearer in another season. Conservation Its global category is Least Concern, while habitat deterioration, pesticides and illegal hunting remain local pressures. Retaining diverse field margins, shrubs and insect food supports birds through different stages of their lives. Where agricultural conflict occurs, assess actual damage and seek lawful, selective solutions that consider other species rather than targeting unidentified mixed flocks. Watching from outside a breeding colony or roost avoids disturbing hundreds of birds for a single close photograph. articles.title: Spotted Crake
articles.body: Spotted Crake Porzana porzana Identity and identification The Spotted Crake is a small, compact Rallidae species with a short yellowish bill tinged red at the base and greenish legs. White spotting marks the head and body, with barring on the flanks. Its short bill contrasts with the long bill of Water Rail. Habitat and food It uses shallow marshes and vegetated muddy margins, feeding on invertebrates and plant material. It often stays concealed, rewarding patient observation at a habitat edge. Breeding and development BTO reports a typical clutch of 10–12 eggs and shared incubation lasting 18–19 days. Downy chicks can move about early, but flight normally develops at 43–56 days. Leaving the nest site therefore differs from becoming capable of flight. Arab occurrence and seasonality Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes common spring passage, scarce autumn passage and rare winter presence from mid-November to late February. Qatar Bird Observation Group lists scarce passage. Winter status should therefore not be transferred from one country to the other. Observation and conservation The species is globally listed as Least Concern (LC) on the IUCN Red List; local habitat protection remains important. The Lebanon guide lists wetland drainage and destruction, together with agricultural expansion, among the main threats. Retaining marsh vegetation and shallow water preserves resting and feeding habitat. Watch without entering reeds or driving birds out for a photograph. articles.title: Squacco Heron
articles.body: Squacco Heron Ardeola ralloides Identity and identification Squacco Heron Ardeola ralloides belongs to Ardeidae. At rest it looks buff-brown, with streaking on head and neck; in flight its white wings are striking. Breeding adults develop longer head plumes, while juveniles are more heavily streaked. Night herons have a shorter-necked appearance and more contrasting dark crown. It is placed in the order Pelecaniformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Shallow water, reedbeds, irrigation channels and marsh margins provide feeding habitat. It waits or walks slowly before seizing small fish, amphibians and aquatic insects. Floating vegetation may serve as a platform; concealment and short strikes replace prolonged pursuit. Breeding and parental care It nests colonially, often with other herons, in shrubs or trees near water or among reeds. Twigs form the nest and both parents contribute to care and provisioning. Young remain dependent around the nest after hatching. Breeding requires relatively undisturbed habitat with reliable food and water. Range and Arab occurrence It crosses North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean and breeds at scattered wetlands within its wider range. Lebanon’s updated checklist calls it a common passage migrant with small winter numbers. The first confirmed Lebanese breeding was documented in May 2020; that local record does not establish widespread breeding. Seasonality and observation Lebanese passage is prominent from mid-March to early June and early August to late September, with a few wintering birds. November sightings therefore require careful documentation but are possible. Seasonality differs among Maghreb wetlands, the Nile basin and the Levant. Ecological role and conservation Its diet connects aquatic invertebrates and small fish with wetland predators. Drainage, polluted channels and disturbance of nesting colonies are pressures. Observe mixed colonies from a distance: adults forced from nests can leave eggs and chicks exposed to heat and predation. articles.title: Tawny Owl
articles.body: Tawny Owl Strix aluco Identity, life and distribution Tawny Owl Strix aluco is a medium-sized owl with a rounded head, no ear tufts and dark eyes. Mottled brown or grey plumage provides camouflage against bark. Colour alone is insufficient to separate it from related owls. It inhabits woodland and mature trees, including large gardens. Mainly nocturnal and usually resident, it retains established territories while young birds disperse. A daytime sighting therefore does not make it a daytime specialist. Small mammals form much of its diet, supplemented by small birds, amphibians, large insects and earthworms. The balance varies with prey availability in its habitat. Tree cavities and nest boxes provide nesting sites. BTO gives a typical clutch of two or three eggs and female incubation of about thirty days. These are reference values, not a fixed schedule for every pair or region. Retaining suitable old trees protects an important part of its habitat. Observe from a distance, without approaching cavities or using playback to attract birds. The photograph illustrates the species and does not document an Arab-world record. Following AviList, the October 2025 Clements update includes Maghreb Owl within Strix aluco as S. a. mauritanica, reversing an earlier split. North African records may therefore use either the species or subspecies name, depending on the checklist; the British photograph here does not illustrate Maghreb plumage. www.bto.org — Tawny Owl · www.rspb.org.uk — Tawny Owl · www.bto.org — Tawny Owl · www.birds.cornell.edu — Tawny Owl Photo: bobhunter2

articles.title: The Silence Horses Speak
articles.body: A bay horse rearing in a green pasture. On those who ride not to arrive, but to remain An hour before the sun finds the stable, someone is already there—a man or a woman who has beaten the light to the door. No cameras. No crowd. No cups lined up on a shelf. Only the smell of hay and damp sand, warm breath rising in the last cool of dawn before the day’s heat, and a hoof that strikes the ground once, as if to say: You’re late. This is the world newspapers rarely show. The world of people who truly love horses—who know a mare is not possessed but companioned, and that trust built over years can collapse in a moment of neglect. In the barns they say horses read their people before their people read them. They catch the tightness in a shoulder, the hesitation in a hand, whatever sits unspoken in the chest. That is why no one lies in front of a horse. Dawn Rituals And this world has its quiet rites. Cleaning a hoof is less a chore than a habit of attention; long grooming is a conversation without words; a leather saddle that softens with the years carries its rider’s memory the way an old notebook does. The rider who starts the day already cantering—before pausing once at the horse’s head to breathe with her—misses half of what he came for. There is elegance in this life that has nothing to do with extravagance. It is the elegance of what lasts: riding boots you care for over ten years until they grow more beautiful; a light linen shirt that takes in morning sweat and the scent of horses together; a simple stable kept as ordered as a reception room. Luxury, here, is having time—and spending a full hour on a creature that thanks you only with a look. A white horse galloping across open pasture. Heat as Teacher In our countries, heat governs the stable. People who truly love horses do not fight the heat; they make peace with it and learn its rhythm: When to ride: Early dawn and late afternoon belong to horse and rider. The hours between are for shade and rest. Water first: A horse drinks tens of liters a day—more in hot weather. Water should be clean, as cool as practical, and always available. On long, hard work, salts (electrolytes) are added under a veterinarian’s guidance; sweat takes more from the body than water alone. Cooling after work: Do not leave a horse suddenly after effort. Walk until the breathing settles, then wet the body and legs with lukewarm or cool water and scrape the excess so heat does not stay trapped against the skin. Warning signs: Breathing that stays rapid, sweat that suddenly stops, or unusual lethargy. These can signal heat stress; calling the vet then is not something to postpone. When to call the vet Rapid breathing that will not settle, sweat that suddenly stops, or unusual lethargy can signal heat stress. Do not postpone the call to your veterinarian. General practical guidance — not a diagnosis. Sand and its risks: Sandy ground looks soft, but a horse that eats feed off the ground may swallow sand with it and develop what is called sand colic. Better to offer feed in raised mangers or on mats, and keep fiber intake regular. Soft sand is not always harmless A horse eating feed off sandy ground may swallow sand with it. Offer feed in raised mangers or on mats, and keep fiber intake regular. Any suspected colic = veterinarian at once. No DIY electrolytes without guidance. The hoof: Severe dryness makes the hoof brittle. It needs balanced moisture and regular farrier care—not an excess of products. This is knowledge horse people learn by living with animals—knowledge our ancestors mastered in the desert long before it was written down. Arabian horses, long known for patience and for enduring hard ground, answer care with a loyalty few other creatures match. People of the Land, People of the Sky Those who know horses know the land as well: which pastures ripen first, which tracks soften under a hoof, which way the wind arrives. Very often a lover of horses is also a lover of birds—from the falconer with a bird on the forearm to the rider who stops to watch a flock cross at sunset—because both have learned to listen: to a distant neigh, or to a wing cutting the air so that the mare turns her ears before anyone has seen it. Some say horses teach patience. More truly, they teach presence. When you ride a mare across open ground at the golden hour, and the sun descends in honey light over the dunes, there is no inbox left in your head, no appointments—only the rhythm of four hooves, the warmth of a body beneath you, and a horizon that approaches without hurry. That is what it means to belong to horses: to know that the finest part of riding is the stretch of time when you do not seem to be going anywhere at all.

articles.title: Touqi Season highlights wildlife and birds at King Abdulaziz Royal Reserve
articles.body: Gazelles at King Abdulaziz Royal Reserve, in an archival image. The King Abdulaziz Royal Reserve Development Authority inaugurated the second Touqi tourism season on 8 October 2026. Running through April 2027, it forms part of Saudi efforts to develop ecotourism while protecting wildlife and natural habitats. The new season builds on its first edition, which welcomed more than 20,000 visitors over 78 days, and expands nature, adventure and heritage experiences as well as opportunities for local communities. Nine bird species added to the reserve records Last summer, the authority also announced a scientific milestone: nine bird species had been documented within the reserve for the first time. The findings were based on a year-long field survey and published in the peer-reviewed journal Check List in June 2026. Researchers from the authority and King Saud University surveyed terrestrial, aquatic and migratory birds, including occasional visitors outside their usual migration routes. The species included the lanner falcon, long-eared owl, rosy starling, yellow-throated sparrow, black-headed bunting, slender-billed gull, Eurasian dotterel, spur-winged lapwing and greater flamingo. A wadi and watercourse in King Abdulaziz Royal Reserve, in an archival image. Photo source: Saudi Press Agency (SPA) / King Abdulaziz Royal Reserve. Covering more than 28,000 square kilometres, the reserve has vegetated valleys, wetlands and reservoirs behind dams that provide habitat for wildlife and migrating birds. Together, scientific monitoring, conservation and regulated ecotourism illustrate how protected areas can help sustain biodiversity while allowing visitors to discover it. articles.title: Turtle Doves Cross Hunting Borders: One European Flyway Recovers, Another Remains Under Pressure
articles.body: European Turtle Dove in Algeria.Photo: Mourad Harzallah / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0. European countries have cut Turtle Dove hunting by about 90% across the two main flyways they manage. Yet the bird's breeding population has followed different paths: growth in the west, and a continued decline with signs of stabilisation in the central and eastern flyway. What does that divergence tell us about managing a bird whose journey crosses borders? A July 2026 report from the European Federation for Hunting and Conservation (FACE) paints a mixed picture for the European Turtle Dove (Streptopelia turtur). The population breeding on the western flyway has continued to increase: its spring 2025 index was the highest since 2009. On the central and eastern flyway, the long-term trend is still downward, though the index has shown signs of stabilising since 2021. Hunting has fallen by about 90% on both flyways compared with the respective baselines used by the management programme. In 2025, western flyway countries reopened hunting under small quotas after a four-year moratorium; quotas on the central and eastern flyway remained low. Countries require hunters to report their take, with several using digital systems to track quotas. FACE argues that the continuing decline in the central and eastern flyway, despite the large reduction in hunting, warrants closer study of other pressures, especially the habitats Turtle Doves need to breed and feed. This finding does not mean hunting has no effect. It means reducing it alone has not yet produced a recovery comparable to the one observed in the west. Where do Arab countries enter the story? The bird's migration extends beyond the European scope of the FACE report. The western route crosses the Iberian Peninsula, Morocco and Mauritania towards Africa. Other routes pass through Italy, Malta and Tunisia, or through Greece, Egypt and the Levant, including Lebanon. Breeding grounds in Europe, stopover sites and wintering grounds in Africa are therefore parts of the same story. For Arab hunters, the report points to a practical question: how many Turtle Doves pass through each season, how many are hunted, and what is changing in farmland and resting habitats? The European experience demonstrates the value of regular counts, trackable quotas and measuring the results of management decisions year by year. Assessing the species in our countries requires local data and cooperation among the countries on its routes. Sources: FACE Turtle Dove Report 2026; Bird Migration Atlas; International Single Species Action Plan.
