articles.title: Wallcreeper
articles.body: Wallcreeper Tichodroma muraria Identity and names A flash of crimson against a grey cliff can reveal the Wallcreeper, Tichodroma muraria, a small passerine in the family Tichodromidae. French calls it Tichodrome échelette; Arabic references use متسلق الجدران, متسلق الحيطان or متسلق الصخور. These names describe one species, not several cliff birds. The Lebanon guide gives a length around 16.5 cm, wingspan around 28 cm and weight around 18 g. Such figures describe approximate size rather than measurements expected from every individual. Identification At rest, the bird can blend surprisingly well with rock. Grey body plumage contrasts with black flight feathers, white spots on the outer wing and conspicuous red areas revealed when the wings open. The long, slender, downcurved bill is another useful character. Frequent wing-flicking produces brief flashes of colour as it climbs. A breeding male has a black throat, but this becomes pale in winter; females also have a pale throat outside breeding. A pale-throated November bird therefore cannot be sexed simply by the absence of black. Habitat and food The essential habitat is a rock face with fissures that shelter food. Mountain cliffs, ravines and precipices are typical, while lower cliffs, quarries and substantial stone buildings may be used outside the breeding season. The bird probes cracks for insects and other invertebrates, including spiders, rather than switching to a seed-based winter diet. It may also catch insects in flight. Watching it move slowly across a wall reveals how apparently bare rock can contain feeding opportunities hidden from an observer standing below. Range and Arab occurrence The species occurs through mountain systems from southern Europe towards central and eastern Asia, but its Arab distribution requires careful qualification. Birds of Lebanon 2026 describes an extremely rare winter visitor and only a possible scarce breeding resident. That wording does not establish confirmed Lebanese nesting. Avibase’s Morocco checklist marks it Rare/Accidental, so the country should not be presented as a regular winter stronghold. The occurrence of suitable cliffs alone cannot establish presence. A winter record also says little about where that individual bred. Breeding and development Where breeding is established, a deep crevice or cavity shelters the nest, usually on a mountain cliff. The female builds it with plant fibres and other soft material. Specialist accounts describe about four eggs, female incubation lasting roughly 18–20 days, and young becoming capable of flight at around one month. Both parents feed the brood and care continues after departure. These general figures concern the species’ breeding biology; they should not be turned into evidence of reproduction at an Arab wintering locality or applied as an identical calendar across mountain ranges. November and responsible observation November brings a useful change in the observer’s search image: some birds descend from high breeding areas to lower rock faces. This altitudinal movement is documented in European mountain populations, but does not promise a sighting in every nearby country. Scan a cliff in sections and wait for movement or a red wing-flash. Keep away from edges, climbing routes occupied by birds and suspected cavities. Do not use playback to draw a rare visitor closer. Record the location, elevation, date and behaviour without advertising a sensitive nest site. Conservation Wallcreeper is globally Least Concern. Nevertheless, specialized rock habitats can be damaged, and an elusive species can be difficult to count accurately. The Lebanese guide lists habitat loss and degradation, hunting and disturbance associated with quarrying or climbing. Protecting a site means considering the entire face and its crevices, not merely the point where the bird was photographed. Observation at a distance allows feeding to continue and avoids turning an exceptional encounter into repeated disturbance. articles.title: Wanaameen wins Prince Mohammed bin Saud Al Kabeer Cup prep by 15 lengths
articles.body: Wanaameen in the Prince Mohammed bin Saud Al Kabeer Cup preparatory race, Riyadh, 24 October 2026. The Saudi-bred horse dominates the 2,000-metre finale as Camilio Ospina completes a treble at King Abdulaziz Racecourse. Wanaameen won the Prince Mohammed bin Saud Al Kabeer Cup preparatory race by 15 lengths at King Abdulaziz Racecourse in Riyadh on Saturday, 24 October 2026, covering 2,000 metres in 2:10.649 in the evening’s finale. Camilio Ospina rode the four-year-old Saudi-bred horse for trainer Bader Rizaiq and the sons of King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz. Shadow finished second and Kaflahom third, according to the Jockey Club of Saudi Arabia’s official results. The race offered SAR 120,000 in total prize money, including SAR 60,000 for the winner. It was a preparation for the cup, not the cup race itself, and concluded a 12-race dirt card. A treble for Ospina The victory completed a treble for Ospina, who had earlier won race five over 1,400 metres on Allah Yahyiha and race nine over 1,800 metres on Majaal. All three horses are owned by the sons of King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz; Hesham Abdulwahed trained the winners of races five and nine. In race eight, an open race, Ya Dar won under Ricardo Ferreira for trainer Abdullah Alsidrani, completing 1,600 metres in 1:43.864. The race carried a SAR 120,000 purse, with SAR 60,000 going to the winner. Arabian and locally bred winners Baseq And Bake opened the meeting with victory in the 1,200-metre open Arabian race, ridden by Ricardo Ferreira and trained by Bassim Almousa, in 1:22.630. In race ten, for Arabians over 2,000 metres, Algheed won in 2:23.044 under Fawaz Alshammari for trainer Reyaan Alibrahim. Among the locally bred runners, Dahmat Alwadi won race six, an open contest for two-year-olds over 1,600 metres, under Eddie Castro for trainer Abdulaziz Alhzabi. Ghala Wateen took race eleven, a 2,000-metre maiden for locally bred horses, in 2:14.040 with Mohammad Alyami riding for trainer Mana Saleh Alzamanan. The meeting continued the 2026–2027 Riyadh racing season, which opened at the same racecourse on 16 October. articles.title: Western Reef Heron
articles.body: Western Reef Heron Egretta gularis Identity and identification Western Reef Heron Egretta gularis belongs to Ardeidae. Dark-grey and white forms occur; a white throat patch often marks the dark form. The bill is relatively substantial and the feet yellow. White birds resemble Little Egret, so body colour alone is insufficient; hybridisation can complicate identification. It is placed in the order Pelecaniformes. Habitat, food and behaviour It feeds along shallow coasts, tidal flats, mangroves and exposed reefs. Small fish, crustaceans and other invertebrates are captured by walking or waiting. Tides determine access to feeding places. Short pursuits and wing shading may help locate or catch prey. Breeding and parental care Nests stand near the coast in mangroves, shrubs or other secure sites. References reviewed in a 2025 study of incubation behaviour in eastern Saudi Arabia give typical clutches of three or four eggs and incubation around 26–28 days, with both parents contributing to care. These reference durations vary among populations and are not a fixed calendar for every colony. Range and Arab occurrence Western populations occur along African coasts; eastern populations occupy the Red Sea, Gulf and Arabian Sea region. It is a documented coastal breeding bird in the UAE, including studied mangrove colonies. An identification photograph alone cannot establish occurrence or breeding in another country. Seasonality and observation Resident coastal sites support year-round observation, while numbers and gatherings vary with feeding and breeding conditions. Low tide reveals feeding grounds. Approaching nesting islands must not force adults from their nests. Ecological role and conservation Healthy coasts, mangroves and shallow water sustain it. Mangrove loss, tidal-flat reclamation, oil pollution and colony disturbance are direct pressures. Protecting a nesting colony also requires protecting its feeding grounds: retaining a tree cannot compensate for losing the surrounding tidal habitat. articles.title: White-throated Dipper
articles.body: White-throated Dipper Cinclus cinclus Identity, life and distribution White-throated Dipper Cinclus cinclus is a compact, short-tailed songbird. Adults are dark with a white throat and chest. Despite its diving habits, it is not a member of the waterbird family of grebes. It forages underwater for small invertebrates in fast streams and moves between rocks close to the water surface. Its habitat depends on the food and shelter provided by a river channel, not simply the presence of water. BTO reports a typical clutch of four or five eggs. Sheltered sites beside water, including suitable artificial structures, can provide nest locations. Do not approach nests for photographs. Official French accounts extend its range to northwestern African mountains. Maintaining flow, water quality and riverbanks benefits this ecological specialist. The illustrative photograph does not establish occurrence in a particular Arab river; local records require independent documentation. BirdLife lists Morocco within its native resident range. This presence remains tied to suitable, patchy habitat and does not mean it is common in every Moroccan or Arab river. www.bto.org — White-throated Dipper · faunesauvagedecorse.oec.fr — White-throated Dipper · datazone.birdlife.org — White-throated Dipper · www.mercantour-parcnational.fr — White-throated Dipper Photo: Dario Taraborelli

articles.title: White Wagtail in the Arab World During Migration and Winter
articles.body: White Wagtail From riverbanks and lakeshores to fields and gardens, the White Wagtail draws attention with its long tail and constant movement. Its Arab-world range stretches from Morocco to Egypt, the Levant, Iraq and the Arabian Peninsula, with different patterns of occurrence: passage and wintering in many countries, and local breeding in parts of the range. October offers an opportunity to follow this seasonal presence, whose timing varies between countries. Identification card Arabic name: الذعرة البيضاء English name: White Wagtail French name: Bergeronnette grise Scientific name: Motacilla alba Family: Motacillidae, the wagtails and pipits Length: approximately 18 centimetres, including the tail Arab-world occurrence: passage migrant and winter visitor across extensive areas, with local breeding populations, including the resident Moroccan subspecies Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC) Legal status: the relevant country’s laws and current decisions; global conservation status does not determine whether hunting is permitted When movement provides the first clue A White Wagtail may attract your attention before its colours become clear: quick steps, a short pause, then a long tail moving up and down. This is a useful starting point for identification, provided it is not your only clue. Look at its body shape, colour pattern and movements together; field identification improves when several features are considered rather than a fleeting impression alone. It has a slender body. In the widespread alba subspecies, the back is grey, the underparts white, and parts of the head and breast black. White stands out on the face and along the sides of the dark tail, with white markings also visible on the wings. Its flight follows an undulating path, accompanied by clear, short calls that may alert you to the bird before you see it. Its appearance changes with age and season. In winter plumage, the throat becomes white while a dark mark remains on the breast. Juveniles look duller, with some brownish-grey tones. A broad black breast patch, as shown in breeding-plumage photographs, should therefore not be a requirement before considering White Wagtail as a possibility. Different patterns from Morocco to Oman In Morocco, two patterns overlap: the Moroccan subspecies Motacilla alba subpersonata is a resident breeder, alongside birds arriving on passage and for winter. A wagtail seen there in autumn may therefore belong to the local population or be a seasonal visitor. Winter occurrence is also documented in Tunisia, including sites in the south. Egypt is a country of regular passage and wintering, with field studies documenting the species in the Nile Delta’s agricultural habitats. Farther east, the 2026 Birds of Lebanon guide describes White Wagtail as a common passage migrant and winter visitor, and as a relatively scarce migrant breeder. Regional references also record breeding in northern Iraq. These differences matter: finding a bird in an Arab country during winter does not establish that it breeds there. In the Arabian Peninsula, Saudi surveys confirm winter occurrence, while the Oman Bird List describes it as abundant on passage and in winter. In the UAE, white-faced birds are very common passage migrants and winter visitors from mid-September, mainly October, to April. White Wagtail abundance also varies within a country according to habitat and season; birds may be numerous at one site and absent from another. Interpreting an October sighting October falls within the White Wagtail’s season of occurrence in many parts of the Arab world, but there is no single arrival date that applies throughout. For Egypt, a study published in 2019 places passage and winter occurrence between late September and early May. Lebanon’s passage-and-winter window is wider, from late August to late May, while Morocco’s resident birds must be distinguished from seasonal visitors. An October record should therefore be read with its country, site and date. The wagtail may be passing through, settling for the winter, or a local bird where breeding occurs. One observation cannot reliably distinguish these possibilities; repeated visits and comparison with a local guide are useful. Where to look, and what might cause confusion? White Wagtails use open spaces with short grass or bare ground, including watersides, fields, gardens and areas near buildings. They can appear in places people use every day. An open patch near water is therefore worth a few minutes of quiet watching, without entering private property or approaching sensitive locations. Watch for confusion with Grey Wagtail, Motacilla cinerea, which shows conspicuous yellow beneath its tail despite its name. Yellow colouring can also cause confusion with Yellow Wagtail and closely related species. Do not let a single colour settle the identification, particularly in young birds. Compare the head, breast and tail, and consult a clear photograph or a reliable guide when uncertain. Small prey and a place in the food web Its diet consists mainly of insects and spiders. It picks up prey while walking, makes short dashes after it, and may snatch an insect during a brief flight. Food includes flies, beetles and larvae, including prey associated with water. This diet illustrates its connection to conditions on the ground and along the water’s edge, where its food resources occur. From a habitat-conservation perspective, keeping shores clean and reducing pollution and disturbance benefit the places where birds feed. The presence of one wagtail is not enough to establish water quality scientifically, nor does it allow an estimate of the species’ numbers across an entire area. Its first value is as an observation that can be documented and contribute to systematic monitoring. A wide range and cavity nesting Its Arab-world occurrence is part of a wider range extending across most of Europe and large parts of Asia, with breeding in parts of North Africa and at the margins in Greenland and western Alaska. Migration patterns differ between populations. Geographical forms also vary within the species, so head markings in a Moroccan photograph may differ from those of a wintering bird in the Gulf. It builds its nest in a sheltered place, such as a wall crevice, a cavity or a suitable space in a building. A clutch usually contains four to six eggs. Incubation takes about two weeks, followed by a similar period for the chicks in the nest, and both parents feed them. The nesting season varies by region and population. Global conservation and responsible observation The White Wagtail is classified globally as Least Concern (LC). This assesses extinction risk at species level and does not necessarily describe the condition of every local population. Protecting feeding and nesting places and reducing pollution and disturbance remain important even for a widespread bird. Whether hunting is permitted cannot be inferred from that category. To establish the legal position, consult the relevant country’s laws and decisions in force on the date of the activity, including provisions concerning species, seasons and protected areas. A hunting rule or exception in one country cannot be applied to another. For responsible observation, record the date, place and approximate number, with a photograph showing the identifying features, and let the bird continue feeding. Avoid chasing it for a closer shot. The simple sight of a tail wagging on an autumn shore deserves to be recorded as it is, accurately and quietly. Photo credit: Charles J. Sharp — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0.

articles.title: Wood Sandpiper
articles.body: Wood Sandpiper Tringa glareola — a migrant of pools and flooded fields Identity and name The Wood Sandpiper, Tringa glareola, belongs to Scolopacidae within Charadriiformes, following AviList 2026. Kuwaiti Arabic references use “taytawa al-ghayt”. Its English name does not mean a bird of dry woodland: northern breeding habitats are wet, while passage and winter birds seek shallow water and marsh edges. Distinguishing these seasons explains why a species called “wood sandpiper” may be encountered in a flooded field in an Arab country. Lebanon’s 2026 guide calls it durayjat al-ghab in Arabic. Recognition A slim wader, it has a fine, nearly straight bill, yellowish to greenish legs and a clear pale eyebrow extending behind the eye. Brown upperparts carry pale spots; the underparts are white with breast streaking. Juveniles tend to show more regular buff-toned spotting, while winter adults may appear greyer and less contrasting. Male and female plumage is similar, so photographs should not be labelled by sex without independent evidence. In flight, a conspicuous white rump is visible, but there is no extended white wing stripe. Similar species Green Sandpiper, Tringa ochropus, shows stronger contrast between dark upperparts and pale underparts, relatively shorter legs and a less extensive eyebrow behind the eye. Its underwing is dark, unlike the paler underwing of Wood Sandpiper. Common Sandpiper, Actitis hypoleucos, has a conspicuous white wing stripe in flight and a different structure. Combine eyebrow, body proportions, rump and underwing rather than relying on leg colour altered by light or mud. Identification does not justify deliberately flushing a bird: await natural movement or retain an uncertain identification. Habitats, feeding and breeding It favours shallow freshwater with vegetated edges: pools, marshes and flooded fields rather than exposed marine beaches. It picks insects, larvae and other invertebrates, including worms and molluscs, from the surface or shallow water. Birds occur singly or in small groups, with stopovers providing opportunities to replenish energy. Breeding takes place in northern Eurasian wetlands near woody cover, usually with a ground nest. Downy chicks are mobile after hatching and require safe wet habitat until their flight ability develops. What does a November record mean? Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes common passage on the coast, islands and wetlands, not regular winter visitation. The 2020 checklist places autumn passage from late July to early November, so early November can coincide with its end. Kuwait’s official list calls it a common passage migrant but rare winter visitor; Oman’s database describes abundant passage and winter occurrence. Winter surveys document it in Morocco and Libya, including inland locations, without demonstrating equal abundance between countries. These contrasts show why an Arab-wide seasonal label is misleading: a winter sighting does not establish residency or breeding. Protecting small stopovers Globally it is Least Concern, but drainage, polluted water and the loss of marsh edges still matter. A small safe pool in a dry landscape may be a valuable stopover; area alone does not determine importance. Avoid approaches that interrupt feeding, and retain marginal vegetation instead of clearing every bank. Its consumption of invertebrates places it in a food web, but does not automatically establish control of a particular pest or prove good water quality.
